Executive summary

All six winners who served in the Legislature voted against the 2025 education savings account law at every recorded House and Senate floor stage. The 20 people covered here split on charter schools. Texas AFT endorsed all 14 non-judicial 2026 candidates. The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed all but four. We found no teacher-residency statement from any of the 20.

This document records what 20 Texas Democrats have said and done on public education. They are:

  • James Talarico, the U.S. senator-elect.
  • Seven statewide executive winners: Gina Hinojosa for governor, Vikki Goodwin for lieutenant governor, Nathan Johnson for attorney general, Sarah Eckhardt for comptroller, Benjamin Flores for land commissioner, Clayton Tucker for agriculture commissioner and Jon Rosenthal for railroad commissioner.
  • Four Texas Supreme Court winners: Maggie Ellis, Chari Kelly, Kristen Hawkins and Gisela D. Triana.
  • Five winners for the State Board of Education, the elected 15-member board that sets curriculum standards and approves teaching materials: Thomas Ray Garcia, Coretta Mallet-Fontenot, Allison Bush, Michelle Palmer and Tiffany Clark.
  • Dana Van de Walker, whose board race is not called.
  • Marisa B. Pérez-Díaz and Gustavo Reveles, sitting board Democrats who were not on the ballot.

Hinojosa, Goodwin, Talarico, Rosenthal, Johnson and Eckhardt, the six winners who have served in the Legislature, each voted no on Senate Bill 2 of 2025 at every recorded floor stage. The House Journal and the Senate Journal record those votes. The law created the state's education savings accounts, which are state money a family can spend on private-school costs.

The voucher statements we found for the others who are not judges oppose public money for private-school tuition. Two statements are qualified:

  • Bush's campaign FAQ says public funds "including vouchers" must strengthen classrooms and does not call for repeal.
  • Under a child-care heading, a Texas Tribune guide reports Hinojosa as saying vouchers "should be expanded to include public pre-K programs", without saying which vouchers it means (HPPR).

We found nothing in their own words on vouchers from Clark or Van de Walker. Eckhardt, who as comptroller will run the program, has pledged in The Texan to "audit the daylights out of" it.

Hinojosa has pledged to replace Commissioner of Education Mike Morath with an educator, and in 2021 she filed a bill to make the commissioner an elected office. The pledge is on her campaign site. Her campaign's transcript of her victory speech has her saying, "on day one, I will fire Mike Morath". The 2021 bill was House Bill 613.

No nominee has been named, as the Texas Tribune shows. We found nothing from her on appointments to the State Board for Educator Certification, the governor-appointed board that writes teacher-certification rules. That board is separate from the elected State Board of Education.

We found no statement on teacher residencies from any of the 20.

On charter schools, Talarico wrote in 2022 that high-quality nonprofit public charters have a role, while Goodwin, Rosenthal, Mallet-Fontenot, Palmer, Van de Walker and Reveles have asked for fewer new charters or a pause. Talarico's words were "a role for high-quality nonprofit public charter schools", in a candidate survey on Teach the Vote. The survey and the site belong to the Association of Texas Professional Educators, a teacher association that does not endorse candidates.

Pérez-Díaz called for "a halt to the expansion" in 2018 and later voted to allow several new charters. The board minutes show that Clark and Reveles voted against allowing every applicant on a named roll call in 2025 and 2026 except Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy. Each voted to allow that school and then voted not to veto it.

Hinojosa, Goodwin, Talarico and Rosenthal, the four who served in the House, split on House Bill 4545 of 2021, and all four, with Johnson, voted against House Bill 8 of 2025, the law replacing the state test. House Bill 4545 dealt with retakes and extra instruction for students who fail the state test, STAAR. Talarico voted no in committee and then yes at every House floor vote.

Goodwin and Rosenthal voted no throughout, and Hinojosa voted no and then yes on the final version. On House Bill 8, the 2025 law that replaced STAAR, the four House members and Johnson voted no.

Texas AFT, the Texas affiliate of the national American Federation of Teachers, endorsed all 14 non-judicial 2026 candidates here, and only Talarico has 2026 backing from a reform group. The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed all of them except Flores, Tucker, Rosenthal and Mallet-Fontenot. Talarico's reform backing comes from Democrats for Education Reform, a national group that endorses Democratic candidates.

Hinojosa received the largest direct contributions from teacher organizations that we identified: $250,000 from the American Federation of Teachers' national committee and $250,000 from the National Education Association's.

Larger sums are reported to have gone to outside groups supporting Talarico, not to his campaign:

  • The Houston Chronicle reported that Reed Hastings gave $1,000,000 to outside groups supporting him. The Chronicle did not name the receiving committee.
  • The Texas Tribune reported that Stephen Mandel gave $500,000 to Lone Star Rising PAC, a super PAC that operates independently of his campaign. A super PAC is a type of political action committee.

The Texas Home School Coalition, a home-school advocacy group, endorsed the Republican opponent in each of the 12 statewide races in this document. Those are the races for U.S. Senate, the seven executive offices and the four Supreme Court seats. The coalition also endorsed three Republican State Board candidates: Victoria Hinojosa in District 2, Tiffany Nelson in District 6 and Audrey Young in District 8.

Charter Schools Now PAC, a charter-school political committee, endorsed Greg Abbott and, as a campaign finance report shows, funded four Republican State Board candidates.

We found no statements on education policy by the four judges, Ellis, Kelly, Hawkins and Triana, in the sources we could open. The Code of Judicial Conduct bars pledges suggesting how they would decide classes of cases.

Their record is rulings. One is Triana's 2020 opinion upholding an injunction that the Houston Independent School District won against the commissioner of education's takeover steps. In that takeover, announced in 2019, the state replaced the district's elected board with "an agency-run board of managers", in Teach the Vote's words.

The Supreme Court later reversed and vacated the injunction, noting that the Legislature had since rewritten the governing law.

Implications for the future

On most education questions the Democratic winners want the same things, and in 2027 we expect them to act through the offices they have won. Change will come first through who runs the state agencies and through the budget, which both parties must agree on. Expect few new education laws, because Republicans are projected to keep the Senate, and every new law needs the Senate.

The voucher program stays, but its funding for 2028 and 2029 is undecided

Repeal needs the Senate, and the Senate's Republican majority passed the 2025 voucher law, so we think repeal is very unlikely in the session that ends in May 2027. The law created education savings accounts, state money families can spend on private-school costs. All six winners who served in the Legislature voted against it, and Hinojosa, the governor-elect, has pledged to end it.

In Arizona, Governor Katie Hobbs tried in her first year to repeal the universal part of her state's program and failed against Republican lawmakers.

Eckhardt becomes comptroller, the statewide official who runs the voucher program and also estimates the state's revenue. We think it very likely that she keeps it running through the 2026-27 school year and audits it by August 2027, as she has pledged. We rate it uncertain whether the budget settled by June 2027 includes money for the program in 2028 and 2029, because House budget writers, the governor and the Senate all shape that budget.

The first sign to watch is the six repeal bills filed on November 9, 2026, none yet in committee.

The 2025 teacher raises keep their funding, and a new raise is uncertain

Current law already requires districts to keep paying the teacher raises in the 2025 school finance law, so we think it very likely that they stay funded in the budget settled by June 2027. Each winner who voted on that law voted for it at least once, and the Senate passed it 31 to 0.

That vote also tells us the Senate is not a known opponent of raises. Even so, we rate a new across-the-board raise by June 2027 uncertain. Hinojosa has pledged higher teacher pay but named no dollar figure.

The open questions are money and what each chamber asks in return. Spending bills normally must fit within the money the comptroller says the state will have. Watch the comptroller's revenue estimate in January 2027, and then the House's first budget.

Hinojosa's choice likely runs the education agency, and the 2025 testing law stays

We think it likely that by May 2027 Hinojosa's choice for commissioner of education runs the Texas Education Agency, the agency that oversees public schools, confirmed or serving while the Senate decides. Confirmation by May 2027 is uncertain. On projected results it needs at least nine Republican senators if every senator votes.

The Senate passed the 2025 testing law 21 to 5. A law cancelling its tests or pausing the A to F ratings, the state's school letter grades, is very unlikely by August 2028.

A pause without a new law is also very unlikely by August 2028, since the law requires yearly ratings with listed exceptions. The commissioner can change the standards or measures behind them, which we think likely by then if Hinojosa's choice is in office.

In Houston, a state-appointed board of managers replaced the elected board, and Hinojosa has pledged to restore the elected board. In a May 2025 letter the current commissioner promised to announce a timeline on or around June 1, 2027, so we think that announcement very likely by the end of 2027. Elected trustees holding every seat by then is very unlikely.

No charter pause becomes law, and more State Board vetoes are uncertain

A binding pause on new charter schools, publicly funded schools run under a state charter, would need a new law that passes the Senate, so we think it very unlikely by May 2027. The people covered here split on charters.

Talarico, the U.S. senator-elect, wrote in 2022 that high-quality nonprofit charters have a role. Goodwin and Rosenthal asked for fewer new charters or a pause, and so did four Democrats who sit on or ran for the State Board of Education, the elected 15-member board that sets curriculum.

That board can veto a new charter the commissioner proposes. Whether it vetoes more of them by the end of 2027 is uncertain. Two Democratic members voted against nearly every applicant in 2025 and 2026, while a third voted to allow several.

The parties hold seven seats each, and District 8, the one board race not yet called, decides which party has eight. The final count there, due by December 7, 2026, will settle that question.

The Ten Commandments law stays, but the attorney general likely stops arguing for it in court

Repeal of the 2025 Ten Commandments law, which requires the commandments to be displayed in classrooms, needs the Senate, so we think it very unlikely by May 2027. Repeal of the 2023 and 2025 laws on school library books is also very unlikely by then. Hinojosa and Johnson voted against the Ten Commandments law.

Johnson becomes attorney general, the official who represents the state in appeals. As a candidate, he said he would not defend the law because he considers it unconstitutional. So we think it likely that his office stops arguing for the law in court by the end of 2027.

That would not repeal it, and schools must still comply unless a court blocks it.

The State Board's 2026 social studies standards and its reading list with Bible stories stay unless a board majority votes to reopen them. We rate that uncertain by the end of 2027, and it depends on who wins District 8.

Teacher certification rules likely stay as they are, and preparation funding continues

We found no pledge from Hinojosa that names a certification rule, program or funding source, so we think a substantial change to the rules for preparing and certifying teachers is unlikely by the end of 2027. We also found no statement from any of the 20 people covered here on teacher residencies, routes built around a supervised year in a classroom before certification.

That silence is not evidence that nothing will change. The governor appoints, with Senate consent, the voting members of the State Board for Educator Certification, which writes the rules, so the estimate depends on who sits on it in 2027. A third of its seats expire on February 1, 2027, and Hinojosa's nominees for them will show which way the rules move.

We think it very likely that the 2025 school finance law's money for teacher preparation programs is funded as designed for 2028 and 2029, in the budget settled by June 2027. Every winner who voted on that law voted for it at least once, and we found no group opposing the funding.

The 2023 and 2025 university laws stay through the 2027 session

Repeal needs the Senate, so we think repeal of the 2023 law on university diversity offices or the 2025 law on faculty governance is very unlikely by May 2027.

Regents govern the state's public university systems. Hinojosa plans to appoint regents who would extend tuition grants to housing, food, transportation and textbooks. We make no estimate on those appointments, because we found too few comparable cases.

The date to watch is February 2027, when a number of regents' seats expire. News reports put the number of expiring seats at 11 or 20.

Dates to watch

  • December 7, 2026: the official count ends and should settle State Board District 8, where the Democrat Dana Van de Walker led by 564 votes in the state's count of November 4. It affects our estimates on charter vetoes and on reopening the curriculum.
  • January 2027: the Senate votes on its rules. We think it likely that Republicans use that vote, by January 31, 2027, to cut the power over committees and bills held by the lieutenant governor, who presides over the Senate. If Vikki Goodwin, who takes that office, keeps those powers, every estimate that needs the Senate becomes less firm.
  • January 2027: the comptroller's revenue estimate sets how much lawmakers can normally spend. It affects voucher funding, a new teacher raise and teacher-preparation money.
  • January to May 2027: the Senate votes on Hinojosa's nominee for commissioner. It affects who runs the agency, confirmation, the ratings and charter vetoes.
  • On or around June 1, 2027: the commissioner announces a timeline for Houston's school board. It affects both Houston estimates.

These are our estimates as of November 9, 2026, no source offers odds, and the rules, sources and reasoning behind each one are in the section "How we made the estimates" under Sources and method.

Teacher preparation and certification across the slate

The State Board for Educator Certification writes Texas's teacher-certification rules, and the elected State Board of Education may reject them but may not change them. Under chapter 21 of the Education Code, the certification board writes the rules for certificates and for the programs that prepare teachers. The same chapter has the governor appoint the certification board's 11 voting members with Senate consent, plus two nonvoting members, one of them from an alternative preparation program.

Every rule the certification board proposes goes to the State Board of Education. Under §21.042, that board may reject the rule by a two-thirds vote of members present and voting within 90 days, but it may not change it.

In June 2026 the board let the rules carrying out House Bill 2, the 2025 school-funding law, take effect on a consent calendar, with no individual votes recorded in its minutes of June 26, 2026. A consent calendar is a set of items approved together in a single vote.

The rules cover the routes into teaching. The committee minutes of June 25, 2026 show that the June 2026 package covered admission to preparation programs, new preparation routes set up by House Bill 2, and intern and aide certificates.

Districts can also avoid some of these rules. Teach the Vote says the Districts of Innovation law lets a district exempt itself from some state requirements, including rules on hiring certified teachers. Teach the Vote is the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE.

The largest alternative-certification provider, A+ Texas Teachers, also known as Texas Teachers of Tomorrow, was in litigation with the Texas Education Agency and the certification board in 2023 and 2024. The dispute concerned its compliance with an agreed order, the docket of the Third Court of Appeals in Austin shows.

17 rows

One question recurs across the record: who should control certification rules. Johnson offered the 2023 amendment to keep the State Board of Education's power to reject them, and Eckhardt voted for it, the Senate Journal records.

On ATPE's Teach the Vote, Bush and Pérez-Díaz have said the board should keep that power. Palmer prefers the elected board to the appointed one. Garcia would give the board power to amend the rules, which the law now forbids.

The other recurring subject is uncertified teachers. Hinojosa, Goodwin, Rosenthal, Mallet-Fontenot, Van de Walker, Pérez-Díaz and Reveles have each addressed them. Reveles is the only one to say they should be allowed in some cases, in the League of Women Voters guide of 2024.

Johnson's 2024 survey answer on Teach the Vote cites the state's figure that 28.8 percent of new teachers hired in 2022-23 were uncertified.

We found nothing on teacher preparation or certification for Benjamin Flores, Maggie Ellis or Kristen Hawkins.

For the four judges, the absence of teacher-organization backing is the finding. The Texas AFL-CIO, a labor federation that includes teacher-union affiliates, endorsed all four on July 21, 2026. That is a labor endorsement rather than an education one.

An Austin law firm with school-district and higher-education practices gave Kelly $1,030 and Triana $1,000 on November 27, 2023, in an earlier election cycle for the Third Court of Appeals.

Education-oriented groups also backed the opponents. Charter Schools Now PAC endorsed Greg Abbott, the Abbott campaign says. The American Federation for Children, a school-choice group, endorsed him on February 10, 2026, a second Abbott campaign release says.

The Texas Home School Coalition endorsed the Republican opponent in each of the 12 statewide races in this document, as its list shows. In the U.S. Senate race it endorsed Ken Paxton. In the seven executive races it endorsed Greg Abbott, Dan Patrick, Mayes Middleton, Don Huffines, Dawn Buckingham, Nate Sheets and Bo French.

For the four Supreme Court seats the coalition endorsed Jimmy Blacklock, James P. Sullivan, Kyle Hawkins and Brett Busby. It also endorsed three Republican State Board candidates:

  • Victoria Hinojosa, Garcia's opponent in District 2.
  • Tiffany Nelson, Palmer's opponent in District 6.
  • Audrey Young, Van de Walker's opponent in District 8.

Charter Schools Now PAC gave $2,500 to Victoria Hinojosa, $1,000 to Tammie Nielsen, Mallet-Fontenot's opponent, and $2,500 plus $32,483 in in-kind ads to Tiffany Nelson, as two campaign finance reports show. It gave $5,000 to Audrey Young in April 2025, as an earlier report shows.

The same committee also endorsed and funded Bush's Democratic runoff opponent, Stephanie Limon Bazan. Commit to Students PAC, a Dallas committee whose purpose was not established, gave Dan Patrick $5,000.

Two groups that appear in the profiles do not endorse candidates. The Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association, says on its ATPE-PAC page that its political committee's contributions "do not constitute a public endorsement by ATPE". That committee gave to Hinojosa's 2026 campaign for governor, Bush's 2026 State Board runoff campaign and Talarico's earlier Texas House campaigns, and those items appear here as contributions.

Raise Your Hand Texas, a public-education advocacy group, says on its website that it "will not endorse candidates". The Charles Butt Public Education PAC, which gave to Talarico's House campaigns, is a separate committee, and we did not establish a link between the two.

Texas Parent PAC does endorse candidates. In the 2026 primaries it endorsed only Hinojosa.

Statewide executive offices

Gina Hinojosa, Governor

The Associated Press called the race for Hinojosa over Greg Abbott, the incumbent, and the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data, carry that call. The Texas Secretary of State's unofficial results show the count. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Hinojosa voted against the 2025 education savings account law at both House floor stages and pledged as a candidate to end the program.

The governor appoints the commissioner of education, who runs the Texas Education Agency. The governor also appoints the voting members of the State Board for Educator Certification, which sets teacher-certification rules.

Hinojosa has been in the Texas House since 2017. She voted no on Senate Bill 2, the voucher law, at second and third reading on April 17, 2025. She voted against House Bill 8, the 2025 testing law, at second reading, third reading and concurrence. Her campaign site pledges to end the state's standardized test.

Her campaign site calls her "a negotiator of the historic 2019 school finance bill," but Texas Legislature Online does not list her on that bill's conference committee.

Her most detailed statement on certification is a 2024 letter calling for a reversal of the decline in certified teachers. We found no pledge that names a certification rule, program or funding source.

Background and powers of the office

Hinojosa won an at-large seat on the board of the Austin Independent School District, or Austin ISD, in November 2012. She was board president from January 2015 until December 15, 2015, Austin ISD announcements of January 7, 2015 and December 14, 2015 show. She gave up the presidency on December 15 to run for the Texas House.

She left the board in November 2016, an Austin ISD announcement shows. She has represented House District 49 in Austin since January 10, 2017, the Legislative Reference Library records. She launched her campaign for governor in Brownsville on October 15, 2025, her campaign release says.

  • Education roles. Texas Legislature Online for the 88th Legislature lists her in 2023 on the House Public Education Committee and on the Select Committee on Educational Opportunity & Enrichment. That select committee was the House's 2023 interim committee on vouchers. She sat on Public Education again in 2025, the committee minutes of April 3, 2025 show. In 2019 she chaired the House Democratic Caucus Special Committee on Public Education, a working group of House Democrats.
  • The commissioner of education. The governor appoints the commissioner who runs the Texas Education Agency, or TEA, the state agency that oversees public schools. The Texas Tribune reported on November 5, 2026 that "Hinojosa must appoint someone and submit the name to the Texas Senate for official confirmation". The Tribune describes that confirmation as needing a two-thirds vote.
  • Budget veto and the State Board of Education. The governor can veto single budget items, such as funding for the education savings account program, according to the same Tribune article. The governor also names the chair of the elected State Board of Education from among its members, the article says.
  • Educator certification. The governor appoints the voting members of the State Board for Educator Certification, which sets the rules for teacher certification and for the programs that prepare teachers, under chapter 21 of the Education Code. Under section 21.033, the governor appoints, with Senate consent, the board's 11 voting members: four public-school teachers, two administrators, one counselor and four citizens. The governor also appoints two nonvoting members, a dean of a college of education and a person from an alternative educator preparation program.

We could not read her X accounts, @GinaHinojosaTX and @GinaForAustin, because X returned an access error. We did not retrieve Instagram or Facebook, which require a login. All posts below are from Bluesky.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

She has pledged to end the education savings account program. Her campaign site, in a page last modified August 11, 2026, says "Gina will end the voucher scam and ensure Texans' taxpayer dollars go where they belong".

The program she refers to is the education savings account program created by Senate Bill 2 in 2025, which uses state money for private-school costs. The Texas Tribune of November 5, 2026 carries her words at a September 2026 press conference: "We cannot afford to take $4 billion to give to this unaccountable voucher scam, so I will block that."

On February 5, 2026, she told Austin PBS, "I believe we can undo vouchers." Her reason, in the same interview, was that some House and Senate Republicans want to undo them but "do not feel free to vote their conscience".

Statement or interview

The four statements below, from 2016 to 2026, oppose vouchers.

  • In her 2016 ATPE survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I will not support any proposal to create a voucher, or a neo-vouchers program in Texas."
  • On October 19, 2023, she said, "The Governor's bribe is immoral," in a Center Square story carried by the Washington Examiner. Abbott had offered to add teacher pay to a special session once education savings accounts passed.
  • On April 17, 2025, in the final House debate on Senate Bill 2, she said, "This bill is everything that is wrong with politics."
  • On Election Day, November 3, 2026, she cited her work with House Republicans as the model for her governorship: "In 2023, we stopped vouchers."

Social media

  • On February 6, 2025, she posted: "If 5.5M public school kids must take it, so should everyone in taxpayer-funded education, including wealthy families taking a voucher".
  • On January 17, 2026, she posted that "every time they talk about 'school choice' they are actually taking options away from Texans".

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

She has pledged higher teacher pay and more local control of district spending. Her campaign site pledges to "audit and terminate" vendor contracts and to "use that money to pay teachers to be among the highest paid in the nation". The site gives no dollar figure.

In her signed 2026 survey for the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, on its Teach the Vote site, she wrote: "I will also reinstate local control to allow districts more autonomy in how they spend their tax dollars." ATPE is a teacher association that does not endorse candidates.

Statement or interview

Her funding statements cover recapture in 2016, the 2019 school finance law and teacher base pay in 2026. Recapture is the system that sends part of property-wealthy districts' school taxes to the state. As an Austin ISD trustee, she described it in Spectrum News on May 10, 2016: "It's about $1,000 for the average property taxpayer in Austin that goes directly to the State of Texas to pay for public education elsewhere."

Statement or interview

  • The 2019 school finance law (House Bill 3). On April 3, 2019, she said of the bill, "To the teachers who dedicate their working lives to our kids, who for too long have been under-appreciated and unheard: We hear you, and this bill is for you." Her campaign site says "Gina was a negotiator of the historic 2019 school finance bill." Texas Legislature Online for the 86th Legislature does not list her on that bill's conference committee. Her own 2019 recap, in an archived newsletter, credits "the HB 3 conference committee members". It describes her role as "heading up the House Democratic Caucus' Special Committee on Public Education".
  • On June 2, 2026, preferring higher base pay to the Teacher Incentive Allotment, the state's performance-based teacher pay program, she said in Spectrum News: "We need to do something about base pay so that we can impact all teachers."

Social media

  • On January 28, 2025, she posted about the basic allotment, the per-student base amount in the state formula: "That's how much TX needs to increase basic allotment (per student funding) just to get back to 2019 spending power". The post refers to $1,340.
  • On October 22, 2025, she posted of Texas teachers: "they should be among the best paid in the nation".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

She has pledged to end the state test, to give districts the state took over back to their communities and to replace the commissioner of education with an educator. Her campaign site says "Gina will end the STAAR test and tests like it, pause the rigged A-F accountability system, and call on the Legislature to deliver a bill that creates real accountability".

STAAR is the state's standardized test, written by TEA, Texas Standard explained on October 23, 2026. The A-F system is the letter grade the state assigns each school and district, the same story said.

The same campaign page pledges, "Gina will return school districts that have been taken over back to their communities". The page also pledges to replace Commissioner Mike Morath with an educator because "the agency that oversees our children's education should be led by someone who has taught them".

  • On April 8, 2026, during STAAR testing week, she said in a campaign release: "As governor, I will end this testing madness that is hurting our kids and destroying our neighborhood schools."
  • On September 22, 2026, at Houston ISD, a district the state took over, she said in a campaign release: "When I am governor, I will give Houston ISD back to the people of Houston, so that there can be accountability again."
  • In her victory speech on November 3, 2026, as a campaign transcript records, she said "on day one, I will fire Mike Morath" and "your schools will not close."

Statement or interview

She has criticized test-based penalties, the state's 2023 conservatorship over Austin ISD and the 2025 testing law. In 2016 she wrote on Teach the Vote, "Testing should not be a punitive measure used to fire teachers or to close neighborhood schools."

On March 31, 2023, when TEA appointed a conservator for Austin ISD over special education, she said, "I am dismayed by [TEA Commissioner Mike] Morath's decision to install a conservatorship in our school district at this time."

  • On the 2025 testing law, House Bill 8, she argued on August 26, 2025, that TEA "should not be in charge of creating the test." On September 3, 2025, she said, "This is no win. This is a terrible bill."
  • Her campaign site says, "Last year, she successfully reduced the number of STAAR tests our kids take." The record supports this for one test. Her House amendment cut the testing schedule to the federal minimum. The Senate restored the other tests, and the enrolled bill drops only the English II end-of-course exam. The Tribune wrote that "Hinojosa added a provision to get rid of the English II test." She voted against the bill on second reading, third reading and concurrence with the Senate's version, as the vote table below shows.
  • On October 23, 2026, she said of STAAR in Texas Standard: "It is created by the Texas Education Agency that then decides how to grade it after the kids have already taken the test." She added, "We need an objective outside measure of our kids' performance." On Morath, she said in the same interview: "I don't have anything against the man personally, but I do believe we need an educator in that position to get us back on track."
  • On November 5, 2026, the Texas Tribune reported that "her team was "actively interviewing" people to replace Morath". No nominee was named.

Social media

  • On August 26, 2025, she posted: "the House adopted my amendment to cut the number of high stakes tests to the federal requirement".

Charter schools

Statement or interview

She has opposed charter takeovers of local schools and charter admission rules based on discipline history.

  • In December 2012, as a trustee, she spoke on ending Austin ISD's contract with the IDEA charter network: "At some point so much damage is done that it's time for a divorce."
  • In her 2016 survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I do not support allowing charter organizations, management companies, or an achievement authority to take over local schools."
  • Her 2019 newsletter said of her bill to bar charters from refusing students for discipline history: "Public schools take all kids, and so should charter schools."
  • Her campaign site says she "passed legislation to ban charter schools from discriminating against kids because of their disciplinary record". Her own 2025 bill on this, House Bill 1179, did not advance out of committee. A 2025 discipline law by another author, House Bill 6, removed the "discipline problems" exclusion ground. The enrolled House Bill 6 still allows exclusion of a student who "has been convicted of a criminal offense or has a juvenile court adjudication". We did not establish whether she was an author or coauthor of House Bill 6. She voted for it on House second and third reading, as the vote table below shows.

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Statement or interview

She has spoken on critical race theory and on curriculum written by artificial intelligence. At a Texas Tribune event in November 2021, she called "critical race theory" "a made-up issue that is brilliantly used to polarize people". On September 22, 2026, speaking about curriculum generated by artificial intelligence in Houston ISD, she said in a campaign release: "I think that curriculum needs to be made by human beings."

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

We found no pledge that names a certification rule, program or funding source. Her campaign site says experienced teachers "are being replaced by uncertified first-time teachers". That passage ties teacher departures to pay, workload and STAAR.

Her campaign newsletter of August 24, 2026 says "we have to give new educators the support and mentorship they need to become great teachers". The same newsletter says she has "every intention of appointing an educator as head of TEA".

Her newsletter of September 23, 2026, written against instruction led by artificial intelligence, says, "That means having certified teachers at the front of the classroom."

Statement or interview

Her most detailed statement is a signed letter of November 18, 2024, to Brad Buckley, chair of the Public Education Committee. It is printed as Appendix A of the House Committee on Public Education Interim Report 2024.

The appendix pages are scanned images, and the wording below comes from a text-recognition reading of them. In the letter, she wrote that uncertified teachers had "tripled in the last 10 years" and that:

  • "The Speaker's Interim Recommendations appropriately identify "teacher certification" as a goal of our work."
  • "reversing the alarming, precipitous decline of certified teachers in Texas public schools should be the priority of the upcoming legislative session."
  • "But compensation that is dependent in large part on testing performance is problematic"
  • "A qualified, professional teacher in the classroom is foundational to a quality education."

Her other statements on the subject include these:

  • In her 2016 survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I do not support using student scores on state standardized tests in teacher evaluations."
  • In October 2016, as a trustee, she asked that Austin ISD's pilots to reduce the number of ineffective teachers be built with Education Austin, the local teachers union. The Austin Monitor wrote: "Hinojosa asked for this measure to be developed hand-in-hand with Education Austin."
  • Her May 5, 2026 newsletter cited "an alarming 10 point decrease in the number of certified teachers since Greg Abbott has been governor". It gives no source for the figure.
  • Her August 14, 2026 newsletter repeated the "uncertified first-time teachers" line. A September 9, 2026 campaign email used "uncertified, first-time teachers".
  • A June 2, 2026 Spectrum News article that quotes her on base pay also states that "House Bill 2 also banned the hiring of uncertified teachers". That description of the 2025 school-funding law is the reporter's, not hers.
  • Her certification bills and her amendment to a 2023 certification bill appear under "Voting record."

Social media

  • On August 19, 2026, she posted: "No governor in Texas history has driven more teachers away from the classroom than Greg Abbott".
  • On May 4, 2026, she posted: "the best thing we can do for our kids is put a great teacher in the classroom".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

A Texas Tribune affordability guide summarized her plan this way: "She wants to appoint university regents who would expand tuition grant programs to include housing, food, transportation and textbook costs." High Plains Public Radio republished the guide on October 8, 2026. The guide adds that she would have the Texas Higher Education Coordinating Board, a state higher-education agency, investigate rising costs.

Statement or interview

In 2016 the Daily Texan reported that she "believes public universities should have the same right as private universities to opt out of campus carry".

Other

Campaign pledge

The same guide, under its "Childcare" heading, says she "told the Texas Tribune that Texas' vouchers should be expanded to include public pre-K programs". The guide does not say whether "vouchers" means the education savings accounts or child-care subsidies. We did not find her full answer.

Statement or interview

On October 15, 2026, outside the Governor's Mansion, she named raising the purchase age for assault-style weapons to 21 as a school-safety priority after the Uvalde shooting: "That will be my priority. Out of decency for what was lost."

The event was a debate challenge, and, in ABC News 4's words, "Abbott did not make an appearance." No debate took place.

22 rows

Floor amendments she offered. She offered amendments to a 2023 teacher-certificate bill and to the 2025 voucher and Ten Commandments laws.

  • House Bill 621 of 2023 concerned a temporary teaching certificate for veterans without a bachelor's degree. Her Amendment 1 was adopted on May 1, 2023. It limited the certificate to career and technology education and cut its validity from five years to three, as the amendment and the House Journal of May 1, 2023 show.
  • On the same bill, she was recorded as voting no on sending it to third reading. She then filed a statement in the House Journal: "When Record No. 783 was taken, I was shown voting no. I intended to vote yes. Hinojosa"
  • Texas Legislature Online lists her as one of the House negotiators on the bill's conference committee. The enrolled bill covers "creating a temporary certification to teach career and technology education for certain military service members and first responders", valid for three years. She gave no stated reason for the amendment.
  • Her Amendment 18 to Senate Bill 2 of 2025 would have struck the option of "a nationally norm-referenced assessment instrument" so that students using education savings accounts take the state test. It was tabled, the amendment record shows.
  • Her amendment to Senate Bill 10 of 2025, the Ten Commandments law, provided that "the state is liable for the expenses, costs, judgments, or settlements" of school lawsuits over compliance. It was adopted. She then voted against the bill on second and third reading.

Education bills she authored. None of these became law as a standalone bill.

  • She filed a charter-admissions bill every session from 2017 to 2025. House Bill 1179 of 2025 would add "discipline history" to barred admission criteria, its bill text shows. House Bill 43 of 2019 and House Bill 97 of 2021 cleared committee. The last action on each was the committee report being sent to the House Calendars Committee, and neither advanced further. In testimony in April 2021, Raise Your Hand Texas, a public-education advocacy group that does not endorse candidates, said: "Raise Your Hand Texas supports House Bill 97 by Representative Hinojosa".
  • Her pay and funding bills include House Bill 3804 of 2019, an annual cost-of-living adjustment for district employees, and House Bill 4586 of 2023, raising the basic allotment to "$7,075". House Bill 177, filed in the 2023 third called session, proposed a "one-time bonus payment of $15,000" for teachers.
  • House Bill 5419 of 2025 would have audited TEA contracts, capped its staffing and set as a funding priority "attaining and maintaining pay for classroom teachers of at least the national average".
  • House Bill 613 of 2021 would have made the commissioner of education an elected office: "commissioner of education is elected by the qualified voters at the general election". Her 2026 pledge is to appoint an educator. We found no statement reconciling the two.
  • House Bill 4839 of 2023, on educator preparation, would have added to the accountability standards for teacher preparation programs the "quality of a candidate's implementation of the key components of a performance assessment identified by the board". It did not advance out of committee.
  • She coauthored House Bill 1276 of 2019. In districts of 5,000 or more students, no student in grades 1 to 6 could have been assigned two years in a row to a teacher with under one year of experience who "does not hold the appropriate certificate required under Section 21.003". The bill passed the House and did not pass the Senate.
  • House Bill 5282 of 2025 provided that "the agency shall prohibit the use of artificial intelligence" to score written test answers unless validated.

Austin ISD board votes, 2012 to 2016. Her recorded board votes concern the IDEA charter contract, campus plans and the district scorecard.

  • On December 17, 2012, she voted to end the district's contract with the IDEA charter network, which passed 5-4. She voted against an amendment to keep IDEA's grades 6 and 7 at Allan, the Austin ISD Board Briefs record.
  • At the same meeting, the board, including her, "unanimously approved four Annual Academic and Facilities Recommendations", the Board Briefs record. These included an in-district charter at Travis Heights started by the campus.
  • On October 24, 2016, she moved to replace the post-secondary readiness standard with the passing standard in the district's scorecard, and the motion failed.
  • We retrieved no roll call on teacher raises. In June 2015, as president, she proposed raises of 3% for all employees in 2015-16 and 2% the next year.

What was not found

  • We found no statement naming candidates for commissioner of education, and none on appointments to the State Board for Educator Certification or on its rules, before or after the election. We searched coverage from November 4 to 6, 2026.
  • We found no position on alternative certification, online teacher preparation, the certification exemptions that districts can claim as Districts of Innovation, teacher residencies, or the teacher-preparation provisions of House Bill 2 of 2025. Her May 30, 2025 Bluesky post "My statement on HB 2" is an image whose text we did not read.
  • We found no statements on Senate Bill 37 of 2025, faculty tenure or community-college funding.
  • We retrieved no contemporaneous Austin ISD roll calls on school closures from 2012 to 2016. In 2026 she said on KUT of her board tenure, "We saved them. We didn't shut down any schools." We retrieved no closure vote to check it.
  • We found no Raise Your Hand Texas 2026 forum or questionnaire, no League of Women Voters answer and no published Texas AFT or TSTA questionnaires. We could not retrieve a Texas Monthly interview.
  • We did not find the 2019 op-ed "Whose Choice is School Choice?", which her newsletter mentions.
  • We found no Bluesky posts on charters, certification, books or the Ten Commandments.
  • We could not confirm several reported items. One is a quotation on uncertified teachers credited to her in Texas Observer coverage of an April 3, 2025 House Public Education hearing, whose page we could not retrieve. Another is a report that she refused to sign the August 2023 report of the House select committee on vouchers. A third is a report of criticism by the American Federation for Children's chief executive after the election. The last is two X posts on vouchers and takeovers whose text we could not read.

Statewide executive offices

Vikki Goodwin, Lieutenant Governor

The Associated Press called the race for Goodwin over Dan Patrick, the incumbent, as the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data, and the Texas Secretary of State's unofficial results show. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Goodwin voted twice against the 2025 education savings account law and pledged in 2026 not to approve a budget that provides money for private schools.

The lieutenant governor is President of the Senate and, under the Senate's 2025 rules, appoints its committees and refers each bill. The office also co-chairs the Legislative Budget Board with the House speaker. Republicans keep the Senate majority and can change those rules by a simple majority, the Texas Tribune reports.

In the House, she voted no on Senate Bill 2, the 2025 education savings account bill, at second and third reading. She voted for voucher-ban amendments to the 2021 and 2023 budgets. In a 2026 teacher-association survey, she also pledged to end state takeovers of school districts.

On House Bill 1605 of 2023, the basis of the state-written Bluebonnet Learning materials, she voted no, then yes, then no. Her campaign lists House Bill 3103 under a heading on resisting vouchers, but the bill concerns district contracts with out-of-state charter operators.

We found no 2026 pledge on teacher preparation or certification.

Pledges to "raise the basic allotment to previous levels" and index it to inflation (the basic allotment is the state's base funding per student)

Background and powers of the office

According to her campaign biography, Goodwin moved to Austin in 1985 to attend the University of Texas and earned a master's degree in public affairs from its LBJ School in 1991. Her Amarillo Pioneer questionnaire of January 11, 2026 says she is a real-estate broker who owns Goodwin & Goodwin Real Estate.

She won House District 47, in western and southwestern Travis County, in 2018 and has served since January 8, 2019, as the Legislative Reference Library and Teach the Vote record. Teach the Vote is the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association.

She traces her interest in school money to her mother, a trustee of the Dallas Independent School District, or Dallas ISD, who "would complain that there was little local control over money", in a Texas Public Radio, or TPR, and Texas Tribune story of October 15, 2026.

  • Education roles. She never sat on the House Public Education or Higher Education committees. In 2025 she sat on the Appropriations Committee and its subcommittee on Article III, the part of the state budget that funds education, as Texas Legislature Online's page for the 89th Legislature shows. In 2019 she served on the House Democratic Caucus Special Committee on Public Education, her 2019 campaign page says.
  • President of the Senate. The Texas Constitution, article IV, section 16, says the lieutenant governor "shall by virtue of his office be President of the Senate". The same section gives the lieutenant governor the deciding vote when the Senate is tied.
  • Committees and bill referral. Under the Senate's rules, the President of the Senate appoints the Senate's committees and refers its bills. The Senate's 2025 rules, for the 89th Legislature, say: "All committees and standing subcommittees shall be appointed by the President of the Senate, unless otherwise directed by the Senate". Under the same rules, the President names committee chairs and "shall refer each bill to a proper committee". The rules name the Senate's education committee as the "Committee on Education K-16 (11 members)".
  • The budget. "The lieutenant governor and the speaker are joint chairs" of the Legislative Budget Board, a permanent joint committee of the Legislature, under Government Code, section 322.001. Under the same section, the lieutenant governor appoints three senators to the board.
  • Limits. The Senate re-adopts its rules each session. Republicans keep a majority in the Senate, and the Texas Tribune reported on November 5, 2026 that they "only need a simple majority to change to the rules and the authorities they give Goodwin".

General notes

Social media

We checked her Bluesky account, @vikkigoodwintx.bsky.social, and read it in full from November 2024 to November 9, 2026, a total of 429 original posts. We could read her X account, @VikkiGoodwinTX, only through posts embedded in news articles, which are listed above. We did not retrieve Facebook, Instagram, Threads or TikTok. All posts below are from Bluesky. We found no education-specific post between November 4 and November 9, 2026.

Social media

No Bluesky post on teacher preparation or certification was found.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

She pledged to end the voucher program and to approve no budget that funds private schools. In her 2026 ATPE survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote, "I will not approve a budget that provides money for private schools."

In an Amarillo Pioneer questionnaire published January 11, 2026, she listed "Increasing funding for public schools and ending the voucher program" among her top three priorities. Her reason: "Republicans are sending our tax dollars to private schools and as a result, are severely underfunding our neighborhood schools".

She spoke to CBS News Texas the day after the election, in an article of November 8, 2026. She said, "I really want to take the billion dollars that we have going into that ESA program and bring it back into our public schools". She added, "We have a constitutional provision that we have to provide for our public schools". She did not describe a mechanism.

  • Her campaign's education page says "Vikki stood with Democrats and Republicans alike to resist voucher schemes for years" and cites her House Bill 3103 under that heading. The bill itself concerns district contracts with charter operators "not located in this state", not vouchers.
  • The same page says: "Protecting Separation of Church and State – Your tax dollars shouldn't fund religious education."

Statement or interview

Her statements here oppose vouchers or call for a public vote on them.

  • On March 31, 2018, as a candidate, she wrote on her campaign blog: "Vouchers, if passed, would subtract $$ from public schools".
  • On October 12, 2023, she wrote in a signed op-ed in the Austin Chronicle: "I am strongly opposed to taking public tax dollars and spending them on private school tuition." She argued that fewer teachers would weaken the Teacher Retirement System: "we risk a systematic failure of our Teacher Retirement System".
  • On April 15, 2025, she posted on X, as quoted by the San Antonio Express-News: "We should be putting this up for a vote of Texans. That's how we will truly know whether the people of Texas want vouchers." Governor Abbott's office replied, "This is how California is run."

Social media

  • On April 12, 2025, she posted about the House budget: "Ultimately, I couldn't vote for it with the $1 billion for vouchers."

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

Her pledges call for a higher basic allotment, simpler funding and better pay for educators. Her campaign education page pledges to "raise the basic allotment to previous levels, and ensure that future funding keeps up with inflation". The basic allotment is the state's base funding per student. The page cites her House Bill 1770, which would set it at $7,500, and promises "Better Pay for Our Educators".

Spectrum News reported, in its own words, that she would "commit to a 50-50 split between the state and local school districts to fund public schools".

Her ATPE survey on Teach the Vote says, "I plan to increase school funding and simplify the funding formula", and "Schools should have discretion on how to spend their funds". It gives the reason: "The current formula is overly complex, and it was made even more so in 2025."

Statement or interview

In 2018, and again in 2025, she called for more state money per student. On her campaign blog in 2018, she listed recapture among the causes of district cuts: "Rising property values = more $$ going to the state for other school districts". Recapture is the payment some districts send to the state under the school-finance system. On the same blog she wrote, "I pledge to use my budgeting expertise to stop sucking funds from our FREE public schools and increase the per student funding from the state."

A Texas Legislative Council district table shows that her House district includes parts of the Austin, Eanes, Lake Travis, Leander and Round Rock school districts. Her statements on recapture, which she also calls "Robin Hood", changed:

  • In her House newsletter of March 6, 2019, she wrote: "we can't do away with Robin Hood due to our constitution requiring an equitable education system".
  • In her House newsletter of June 6, 2019, she wrote that House Bill 3, which she coauthored, means "all school districts in HD 47 will see a decrease in their Robin Hood recapture payments".
  • On February 11, 2025, she told FOX 7 Austin: "Honestly, if we weren't paying recapture, the state could make up that difference" and "The state isn't paying its share, in our opinion". She also supported a commission on the formula.

Social media

  • On January 24, 2025, she posted: "AISD paid $904M in recapture, or 20% of all recapture paid in Texas in 2023".
  • On May 6, 2025, with House Bill 2 waiting in the Senate, she posted: "The Lt Gov has the power, but not the will."

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

She pledged less testing and an end to state takeovers of school districts. Her campaign education page says: "Less Testing, More Teaching – Our kids and teachers are drowning in STAAR test prep that steals valuable classroom time". STAAR is the state's standardized test. In her ATPE survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I will end the state takeover of school districts and change the law so that can't happen going forward."

Statement or interview

Her statements oppose using tests to set teacher pay or grade schools, and they question state replacement of school boards. In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote: "Standardized tests should not be used to determine teacher pay or to assign a grade to a school."

In July 2024, in a Spectrum News story, she called for an investigation of Houston ISD Superintendent Mike Miles over alleged diversion of funds to a charter network: "This is unconscionable, and should not be allowed".

A machine transcript of a September 21, 2026 podcast interview on The Texan Podcast has her saying "we spend too much time on star [STAAR] testing" and "I don't know that I support closing down schools". In the same transcript she says that TEA, the Texas Education Agency, should support districts "as opposed to coming in and replacing a school board".

Social media

  • On April 24, 2025, when A-F ratings were released, she posted: "Maybe it's our accountability system, or the TX Education Agency, that is failing our students?"
  • On August 27, 2025, she gave her reason for voting against House Bill 8 on second and third reading the day before: "The goal is to remove the high stakes and cut down on time spent teaching to the test. This bill won't accomplish those goals."
  • On March 6, 2026, she posted: "As Lt Governor, I will make sure the state is funding and supporting our school districts, not taking them over. We should not remove locally elected school boards."

Charter schools

Statement or interview

Her statements from 2018 and 2022 criticize charter growth. In 2018 she listed "Charter schools decrease public school enrollment" among the causes of district funding stress on her campaign blog.

In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote that charters were meant to spread innovation, and "This has not happened, and now charters are growing at an exponential rate". She added: "I filed a bill that would provide additional transparency around new charter school locations, and I am in favor or reducing the number of charter schools". Her 2026 campaign materials say nothing about charters.

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Her pledges here concern school libraries and diversity programs. In her ATPE survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I will ensure librarians can do their jobs without fear of retribution."

On October 15, 2026, TPR and the Texas Tribune reported on a panel she spoke at after a film screening on book bans. She said, "Let's go back to that process that we had pre all these book ban bills". According to the same report, she also said she would push "to end the chilling effect and let school districts know that it's fine to have diversity and equity and inclusion".

Statement or interview

Her statements oppose state decisions on specific curriculum, the book ban bills and the Ten Commandments bill.

  • In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote: "The state's role is to fund schools and to provide very broad guidance, but not to make decisions about specific curriculum and instructional materials".
  • In 2026 she wrote on Teach the Vote: "I have opposed the book ban bills since there was already a process for schools to review books when there are complaints." She added, "I also opposed bills that would limit the clubs allowed on campus."
  • A CBS News Texas story on House floor debate in May 2025 on the Ten Commandments bill, Senate Bill 10, has her saying: "it just seems like we're trampling over the freedom of religion by passing your bill".
  • Her three votes on House Bill 1605 of 2023, which led to the state-written Bluebonnet Learning materials, were no, yes and no. She voted no on second reading on May 2, 2023. She voted yes on third reading on May 3 and no on the final version sent back from the Senate on May 17.
  • The Texas Classroom Teachers Association, or TCTA, a teacher association, reported that at the House Appropriations Committee meeting of March 31, 2025, she "had previously expressed concerns with funding for Bluebonnet Learning materials and symbolically voted against the budget as well". We found none of her own words on Bluebonnet.
  • Sherry Sylvester, a former Patrick adviser, said in October 2026, in a TPR and Texas Tribune story: "She is a knee-jerk back bencher whose votes reveal she is a fan of DEI and critical race theory and is fine with … pornography in public school libraries". The House Journal shows that she voted against the 2023 and 2025 library bills. She voted no on House Bill 900 on second and third reading, and on Senate Bill 13 on second reading, third reading and the conference committee report.

Social media

  • On November 25, 2024, listing signs of underfunding, she posted: "Taking bible infused curriculum for $60/student".
  • On March 26, 2025, she posted: "Public school teachers aren't the appropriate people to teach religion."

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

We found no pledge on teacher preparation or certification from her 2026 campaign. We checked its campaign pages and questionnaires.

Statement or interview

Her statements on teacher preparation concern more training, especially for teachers of students with disabilities.

  • Her campaign education page says: "Too many teachers are leaving the profession, and too few college students are choosing to go into teaching." It gives as reasons "Low pay, excessive paperwork, constant testing and safety concerns". It states no certification policy.
  • Her 2022 campaign priorities included: "Provide more training to prepare our teachers to deliver the best education for our students with disabilities."
  • In a 2022 survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "For teachers who work with the population of students needing special education, I will advocate for improved and additional training."
  • A machine transcript of the September 21, 2026 podcast has her saying: "Over half of our teachers now aren't certified. So they don't have the preparation to be as effective as they can be. Maybe we need to make sure that they get the extra training that's necessary so they can handle a classroom". We did not check her figure on the uncertified share.
  • ATPE's vote record lists her as voting in 2019 for House Bill 1276, on certified teachers in the early grades, and House Bill 102, on mentoring. It lists her as voting in 2023 against Senate Bill 798, on school counselors without teaching experience. Those votes are not in the journal records we compiled for this report.
  • Her special-education certificate bills and her coauthorship of a temporary certificate for out-of-state teachers are described under "Voting record."

Higher education

Campaign pledge

The Texas Tribune's affordability guide, republished by High Plains Public Radio, reported that she would "prioritize legislation" that "lowers college costs, including increasing community college funding and expanding college credit opportunities in high school".

Statement or interview

Her one statement here concerns guns at universities. Her 2019 campaign page said her bill would "allow public universities to make the decision whether or not to allow guns on college campuses".

On November 5, 2026, the Texas Tribune wrote that she and Hinojosa "campaigned on K-12 education but offered few specifics about how they would change Texas colleges and universities", in a story carried by KSAT.

Social media

  • On October 15, 2026, she posted: "I've got a plan to make college more affordable and protect free speech for students and professors." We found no plan document on her campaign site.

Other

Campaign pledge

Her campaign pledges wider pre-kindergarten eligibility, and after the election she named no education committee chair. Her campaign's issues page says "Vikki is working to expand Pre-K eligibility to include children of all public school employees", citing House Bill 494. The bill text covers the child of "a full-time employee of the school district".

In the same CBS News Texas article after the election, she said, "I want to make sure that I have conversations with each and every Senator to understand what their district needs". She named no education committee chair or plan for the education savings account program.

Statement or interview

She criticized the 2023 school-safety bill's requirement of an armed person on every campus. She said, "The potential for disastrous consequences is staggering", in the Texas Tribune on May 28, 2023.

No joint debate with Patrick took place. According to TPR's program The Source, Patrick declined.

39 rows

Differences from ATPE's positions. Her votes differed from ATPE's positions on virtual school, two 2023 teacher bills and the 2023 school-safety bill.

  • ATPE opposed the 2021 bills expanding full-time virtual school, as Teach the Vote records. She voted for Senate Bill 15 of 2021 on second and third reading. In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote that virtual school should be "a last resort".
  • ATPE opposed House Bill 100 of 2023 over its condensed salary schedule, and Senate Bill 9 of 2023, the "Teacher Bill of Rights" with a $2,000 stipend, as Teach the Vote records. She voted for Senate Bill 9 on House second reading and for House Bill 100 on House third reading.
  • ATPE supported the 2023 school-safety bill, House Bill 3, as Teach the Vote records. She voted against it at every stage. Her stated objection, in the Texas Tribune, was the requirement for an armed person on every campus.
  • ATPE's entry for House Bill 1605 records her as voting for it. The journal shows the three votes in the table.
  • We found no difference from the positions of Texas AFT or from those of the Texas State Teachers Association, or TSTA. Texas AFT is the Texas affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers.

Her April 12, 2025 post explains a vote against the 2025 House budget over its voucher money. That roll call is not among the journal records we collected for this report.

Education bills she authored. None of her authored education bills became law, as Texas Legislature Online's list of her 2025 authored bills shows.

  • Her bills to raise the basic allotment were House Bill 2139 of 2019, an inflation adjustment only, and House Bill 1107 of 2023, at "$6,500". In 2025 she filed House Bill 351, at "$7,160", and House Bill 1770, at "$7,500" plus an inflation index.
  • Her special-education certificate bill, House Bill 3628 of 2019, was refiled as House Bill 1814 in 2023. It provided that "the board shall establish a special education certificate", with the State Board for Educator Certification setting its exam and preparation-program standards. The 2019 bill cleared committee and did not advance out of the House Calendars Committee. The 2023 bill did not advance out of committee.
  • Her charter-school bills would have set limits on charter bonds, funding and expansion. Under House Bill 3288 of 2019, charter bonds would "be reviewed and approved by the Bond Review Board". That is the state board that reviews certain public bonds under Chapter 1231 of the Government Code. House Bills 2744 of 2021 and 341 of 2023 are titled as funding for small and mid-sized charters. They cap funding for larger charters and set it at "zero if the school has more than 5,000 students in average daily attendance". House Bills 438 of 2021 and 345 of 2023 would limit charter expansion amendments to "Not more than once during each biennium".
  • In 2025, House Bill 3102 would exempt from recapture a district whose enrollment decline is "attributable to students participating in an education savings account program". House Bill 4104 would require the commissioner of education to "remove the conservator, management team, or board of managers" once a taken-over district meets set standards. House Bills 3103 and 494 are described under "Campaign pledges."
  • She coauthored House Bill 3 of 2019, which was enacted. She also coauthored House Bill 4656 of 2023, to "establish a temporary teaching certificate for classroom teachers certified by other states". That bill was left pending in a Senate committee.

What was not found

  • We found no post-election statement naming a chair or members for the Senate Committee on Education K-16, a committee plan, or a plan for administering the education savings account program.
  • No joint debate with Patrick took place.
  • We found no Raise Your Hand Texas forum or questionnaire for lieutenant governor, and no League of Women Voters answer.
  • We found no 2026 campaign statement on charter schools.
  • We found no statement on alternative certification, online teacher preparation, the certification exemptions districts can claim as Districts of Innovation, the State Board for Educator Certification, or the teacher-preparation provisions of House Bill 2 of 2025.
  • We found none of her own words on Senate Bill 17 of 2023, Senate Bill 37 of 2025 or Commissioner Morath by name. On Bluebonnet Learning we have only TCTA's account.
  • For 2021 we found her votes on vouchers but none of her own words on them.
  • We did not find the recapture payments of the Eanes and Lake Travis school districts in her House district.
  • We did not retrieve her Facebook, Instagram, Threads and TikTok posts.
  • Some items were reported but we could not confirm them. One is a post-election television report of her statements on vouchers and on state takeovers of districts. The others are a concession-night quotation on school funding and remarks at a September 2026 forum in Harlingen. None of the pages could be retrieved. Three Texas State Teachers Association pages said to name her in 2026 showed errors when we tried to open them.

Statewide executive offices

Nathan Johnson, attorney general-elect

Result: the Associated Press called the open seat for Johnson over Mayes Middleton, a Republican, as shown in the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data. His margin is 631,187 votes in the Texas Secretary of State's unofficial count. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Johnson voted against the 2025 voucher law at both recorded Senate stages and said as a candidate he would not defend the Ten Commandments law.

The attorney general represents the state before the Texas Supreme Court and courts of appeals. Under Senate Bill 2, the 2025 voucher law, the office represents the state in suits challenging the program's constitutionality or validity. Under Senate Bill 10, the 2025 Ten Commandments law, it defends public schools sued over their compliance.

He voted no on Senate Bill 2 at third reading and concurrence, and on Senate Bill 10 at all three recorded Senate stages. Every voucher statement we found, from 2018 to 2026, opposes vouchers.

In the Texas Tribune's runoff questionnaire, he wrote that the office's duties include defending laws he dislikes but do not require arguing that an unconstitutional law is constitutional. We found no pledge on defending the voucher law.

In 2024 he wrote that he would work for a clear path to teacher certification. His 2023 floor amendment to keep the elected State Board of Education's power to reject certification rules failed, 12 to 19.

Private-school vouchers
Opposed in every statement found, 2018 to 2026; voted no on Senate Bill 2 (2025) twice (Senate Journal)

Background and powers of the office

Johnson is a Dallas trial lawyer at Thompson Coburn and has been the state senator for District 16 since January 2019, as his Senate member page shows. In 2018 he unseated Don Huffines to take the seat, as the Texas Tribune of October 8, 2026 shows. He won the attorney general runoff over Joe Jaworski on May 26, 2026, as CBS News Texas shows.

He never sat on the Senate education or finance committees, as the Senate Education Committee roster shows. His committee assignments in 2023 and 2025 included administration, business, jurisprudence, water and agriculture, and transportation.

The attorney general represents the state in appeals, and two 2025 laws assign the office education duties. Under Government Code §402.021, the attorney general "shall prosecute and defend all actions in which the state is interested before the supreme court and courts of appeals".

The voucher law, Senate Bill 2 or SB 2, says: "The attorney general shall represent the state in any legal action brought that challenges the constitutionality or validity of" the program. The Ten Commandments law, Senate Bill 10 or SB 10, says: "The attorney general shall defend a public elementary or secondary school in a cause of action relating to any claims arising out of a school's compliance with this section".

The office also issues legal opinions on request, including to "a regent or trustee of a state educational institution," under Government Code §402.042. It examines school district bonds before issue, under Education Code §45.005.

The outgoing office sued Frisco ISD, the Frisco Independent School District, in February 2024 for "illegal electioneering". In November 2025 it sued Round Rock and Leander ISDs over Ten Commandments displays, an Attorney General release says.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

We found no pledge on defending the voucher law. In the Texas Tribune's runoff questionnaire of April 23, 2026, Jaworski, not Johnson, listed the voucher bill among laws he would not defend.

Statement or interview

Every statement we found from 2018 to 2026 opposes vouchers.

  • In 2018 his top priorities on Teach the Vote included "Block private school vouchers". Teach the Vote is the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association.
  • On October 13, 2023, his Senate office said in a press release: "A private school voucher program is not fundamental to the function of the state or to the success of public education."
  • In 2024 he answered ATPE on Teach the Vote: "No. I will continue to work hard to stop the turnover of public education to the private sector."
  • On January 31, 2025, he wrote in his campaign journal that "voucher programs do far more damage than good for students, parents, and education".
  • On February 5, 2025, he joined a statement in the Senate Journal calling SB 2 a "voucher scam" that "siphons off billions of taxpayer dollars for private vendors".

Social media

  • Vouchers. On April 15, 2026, his Senate office account posted: "these vouchers would mainly benefit private school kids who can already afford to pay".

School funding and teacher pay

Statement or interview

His SB 233 of 2025 would have raised the basic allotment, the state's base funding per student, "from $6,160 to $7,750 per student", as an office release that his campaign reposted says. In 2024 he wrote on Teach the Vote that he favored indexing the allotment to inflation, because a flat raise "would lose value over time".

In 2019 his office said of property-tax relief and school finance, "Neither can be fixed without the state fulfilling its constitutional responsibility to fund our public education system", in a press release.

His 2025 newsletter says three of his bills "passed as amendments to HB 2," including free pre-kindergarten for teachers' children. That is his own account of provisions in House Bill 2, a larger school finance law. The newsletter adds: "The desire to have a family should not deter good people from becoming teachers or from continuing to teach".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum and religion in schools. His education pledges concern the Ten Commandments law.

  • In an article published April 19, 2026, CBS News Texas quotes him: "I will not defend the legislature's passage of a requirement that schools place the Ten Commandments in classrooms because it's unconstitutional." The article does not give the interview date. Asked whether the state would need private lawyers, he said, "Yes. If they want to defend unconstitutional laws". SB 10, quoted above, makes defending schools under that law a duty of the office.
  • His written answer to the Texas Tribune, published April 23, 2026, separates laws he dislikes from laws he considers unconstitutional. He wrote: "I believe in carrying out the responsibilities of the office, which includes defending laws I may dislike," adding that this "certainly does not mean or require taking the position that an unconstitutional law is not unconstitutional".
  • KTRE reported on May 14, 2026 that he called the ruling of the Fifth Circuit, a federal appeals court, allowing the displays "clearly manipulated to reach a political outcome". In the reporter's words, he would not defend the law while appeals continue.

It wrote in a ballot guide dated July 24 that he "has vowed not to uphold the enforcement of SB 10 (10 Commandments bill) and 11 (mandated school board vote for school prayer)". The guide gives no year. We found no statement of his own on SB 11.

He wrote that "an outright exemption strikes me as potentially reckless." He preferred "a 'loosening' of the margins" and said he would "need to become better informed".

51 rows

On both 2023 votes on HB 1605, on May 12, 2023, and on the 2023 HB 3 conference report, on May 28, 2023, most Senate Democrats voted the other way.

The 2023 amendment on educator-certification rules. On April 6, 2023, Johnson offered an amendment to keep the State Board of Education's power to reject certification rules, and it failed, 12 to 19.

It was Floor Amendment 9 to SB 9, the Senate's 2023 teacher bill, and it would "strike "(1) Section 21.042, Education Code;"" from the bill's list of repealed laws.

Section 21.042 lets the State Board of Education reject, but not amend, a rule of the State Board for Educator Certification by two-thirds of members present and voting. That second board is appointed by the governor and writes teacher-certification rules. ATPE describes the amendment as preserving the elected board's veto over certification rules.

He also voted for Floor Amendment 8, a $10,000 teacher raise, which failed 12 to 19, the Senate Journal records. He voted against SB 9, which passed the Senate 22 to 9, the journal records. SB 9 did not become law.

The Senate Journal and ATPE's record show these other votes:

  • On April 17, 2019, he voted no on taking up SB 1569, a 2019 ban on electioneering by school employees with criminal penalties. After amendments, he voted yes on passage to engrossment and on final passage, the Senate Journal records. ATPE opposed the bill.
  • On April 16, 2025, he voted no on the Senate floor on SB 1962 of 2025, on assessment, accountability and suits challenging the school system, the Senate Journal records.
  • On SB 10 of 2025, he voted yes on the Menéndez and Eckhardt amendments to add other religious texts, which failed 10 to 20, the Senate Journal records.
  • ATPE records that he voted for SB 798 of 2023, on ending the classroom-experience requirement for school counselors, and HB 1468 of 2021, on virtual schools. ATPE opposed both. We did not check the journal for these two votes.
