Statewide executive offices

Sarah Eckhardt, comptroller-elect

Result: the Associated Press called the race for Eckhardt over Don Huffines, a Republican and the appointed incumbent, as shown in the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data. Her margin is 503,311 votes in the Texas Secretary of State's unofficial count. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Eckhardt voted against the 2025 education savings account law at both recorded Senate stages and pledged to audit the program her new office administers.

The comptroller runs the state's education savings account program under Senate Bill 2 of 2025. The office writes the program's rules and certifies the organizations that run the accounts, but the Legislature sets the money. No budget bill passes until the comptroller certifies it.

She voted no on Senate Bill 2 at third reading and on concurrence. The San Antonio Express-News quotes her as a candidate: "I would follow the law, but I would also follow the money vigorously".

She was absent, excused, for the Senate votes on the 2023 bill behind the Bluebonnet Learning materials and the 2025 bill that replaced the state test. Her 2020 platform opposed public money for out-of-district charters and said there is room for in-district ones.

We found no pledge or statement on teacher certification beyond her bills and votes.

Background and powers of the office

Eckhardt was an assistant Travis County attorney, a county commissioner from 2006 to 2013 and Travis County judge, her Senate member page says. The sources differ on the judgeship. The Senate biography dates it 2015 to 2020, and her own releases, such as one of February 13, 2025, say 2014 to 2020.

She won a special election for Senate District 14 on July 14, 2020, the Legislative Reference Library records. She entered the comptroller race on December 8, 2025, after a brief run for Congress, as a Texas Tribune story of that date shows. Her committee assignments in 2023 and 2025 included Local Government, Nominations, Veteran Affairs and Transportation, and she never sat on the Senate education or finance committees.

The comptroller runs the state's voucher program. Senate Bill 2 of 2025, or SB 2, created Texas Education Freedom Accounts, education savings accounts that families can spend on private schooling. It placed them under the comptroller. The enrolled text sets out these duties:

  • Education Code §29.372, in the enrolled text, says: "The comptroller shall adopt rules and procedures as necessary to implement, administer, and enforce this subchapter".
  • Under §§29.354, 29.358 and 29.3585 of the enrolled text, the comptroller certifies the organizations that run the accounts, preapproves providers and vendors, and may suspend them.
  • Under §29.363, "The comptroller shall contract with a private entity to audit accounts and program participant eligibility data not less than once per year", the enrolled text says.
  • Under §§29.366, 29.371 and 29.373 of the same text, the comptroller refers fraud to prosecutors and reports annually on matters including the effect on public-school capacity. The comptroller also makes decisions under the program that are "final and not subject to appeal".
  • Under §29.3521 of the enrolled text, the comptroller's budget request states program costs, but "the amount appropriated … must be established by the legislature by appropriation for that biennium". The program's cap for 2025-27 is $1 billion, a Texas Public Radio story says.

The comptroller also submits a sworn revenue estimate before each regular session. No appropriation bill passes until the comptroller endorses a certificate on it, under the Texas Constitution, art. III §49a. The comptroller conducts the study that determines "the total taxable value of all property in each school district", under Government Code §403.302.

At Governor Abbott's request, the acting comptroller began spending reviews of the Austin, Barbers Hill, El Paso and Prosper independent school districts, or ISDs, in fall 2026. A Texas Tribune story of October 6, 2026 describes the reviews.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

She pledged to audit and report on the voucher program while administering it as the law requires.

  • Her campaign site says: "The Comptroller can protect our schools & audit the voucher scheme".
  • On July 8, 2026, she told The Texan: "We need to audit the daylights out of the voucher system to show who's benefiting most, least, and not at all." She gave the reason: "We cannot afford to subsidize a private elite system for the five percent in private school".
  • In a written questionnaire of October 12, 2026, in the Courier, she wrote: "as Comptroller my responsibility is well laid out in the law." She wrote that she would report "which schools participate, which do not, and what parts of the state have few to no options for utilizing vouchers".
  • In an article of October 14, 2026, the San Antonio Express-News quotes her: "I would follow the law, but I would also follow the money vigorously".
  • KERA quotes her on the program's budget, in a story on the Texas Public Radio site of October 29, 2026: "You don’t haul off and double the funding right out of the gate".
  • On November 4, 2026, the day after the election, she said: "As the comptroller, my job is to vigorously follow the money and report back to the Legislature if their investment is not panning out." Her words appear in the Texas Tribune of November 7, 2026. The Tribune adds that she "acknowledged the limitations of her office, saying that any big overhaul must come from lawmakers".

Statement or interview

Her statements from 2025 and 2026 oppose the voucher law.

  • Her office's release of February 5, 2025 on SB 2 said, "Public dollars should fund public schools". That day she joined the statement in the Senate Journal calling the bill a "voucher scam".
  • Her 2026 newsletter calls SB 2 a bill "which I strongly opposed".
  • After the election, Fox 26 quoted her: "This is a state subsidizing of a private industry that was doing just fine without it".

Social media

  • Vouchers. On April 25, 2025, she posted: "I spoke against SB 2 on the Senate Floor today". On May 8, 2025, she posted: "put guardrails on Abbott’s runaway $1B voucher program".

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

School funding. Her funding pledges concern the Rainy Day Fund and the revenue estimate. She told The Texan the state's Rainy Day Fund "is so big that we could pay down the debt of every single school district that’s running a deficit".

At a Texas Tribune event in late April 2026, she said that she would not be "putting a political thumb on the revenue estimate at any time", as quoted on the event page.

Statement or interview

School funding. Her statements call for full state funding of public education and changes to recapture.

  • On March 22, 2023, she debated SB 4, the school property-tax cut. The Texas Tribune story of that day has her saying, "If for any reason the state is unable or unwilling to pay … it will be a starvation for our public education system," and records that she voted for the bill.
  • In a 2025 release she said: "Texas must fully fund public education, increasing the basic allotment and indexing it to inflation". The basic allotment is the state's base funding per student.
  • Her 2026 newsletter says "Austin ISD is the leader in recapture dollars sent to the State of Texas". Recapture is the payment some districts send to the state under the school-finance system. The newsletter proposes "a discount for districts that submit recapture payments early".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Statement or interview

Her statements criticize state takeovers of districts and the acting comptroller's district reviews.

  • On October 3, 2025, backing Austin ISD's consolidation plan, she wrote in a letter: "In Houston, it took just one school out of 273 campuses with a bad rating for the state to replace the locally elected school board with TEA appointees". TEA is the Texas Education Agency.
  • On August 20, 2026, in Beaumont, she said, in the Beaumont Enterprise: "Standardized testing is a helpful tool. It’s not the only metric of educational success".
  • On October 5, 2026, in Community Impact, she called the acting comptroller's district reviews "political retribution" and "nothing more than the [comptroller] bolstering TEA's favored model of cuts, consolidations, layoffs and takeovers".

Charter schools

Statement or interview

She has opposed public money for out-of-district charters. Her 2020 platform was posted after a charter-school advocacy group announced support for her unasked. It says: "I do not support out of district charters receiving public dollars that would otherwise go to public school districts," and "I think there is room for in-district charters like Travis Heights Elementary School". The archived page names her as the speaker of the first sentence.

Her 2025 letter says state law "has intentionally created an exodus to less regulated charter schools".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Statement or interview

She offered amendments to the 2023 library law and the 2025 Ten Commandments law, and all failed.

  • In 2023 she offered an amendment to House Bill 900, or HB 900, the library-ratings law. It would have required the Texas Education Agency to report "the disaggregated demographic data of" authors or main characters of rated books. It failed 12 to 19, the Senate Journal records.
  • On March 18, 2025, she offered amendments to SB 10, the Ten Commandments law. They would add or substitute a Jewish version of the text, the Five Pillars of Islam, the Seven Core Tenets of Hinduism and the Noble Eightfold Path. All failed 10 to 20, the journal records.
  • She gave her reason for voting no in the Senate Journal: "This bill unconstitutionally establishes the Christian 10 Commandments as the only sanctioned text for mandatory display in Texas public schools".

Social media

  • Curriculum and religion. On March 28, 2025, she posted about her amendment to SB 24 of 2025 on teaching "the horrors of communism": "we should also include the horrors of other authoritarian ideologies". On April 15, 2025, she posted: "not one that dictates religious practices in public schools".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

We found no pledge. The Express-News reported that she is "particularly concerned about schools that rely on artificial intelligence for instruction and replace traditional teachers with adult guides".

Statement or interview

We found no statement beyond her bills and votes below.

Higher education

Statement or interview

Her statements here concern the 2023 university diversity-office ban and the voucher program's effect on university admission. In 2023 she debated SB 17, the ban on diversity, equity and inclusion offices at public universities. A Senate Journal addendum records her telling its author: "I think your bill is concerned that we've made too much progress".

At the LBJ School on March 2, 2026, she said the voucher program would "make it harder for public school students to get into flagship universities", the Daily Texan reported.

45 rows

Most Senate Democrats voted the other way on HB 4545 at third reading in 2021, on the 2023 HB 3 conference report and on both 2025 votes on HB 6. The Senate Journal records these votes for May 27, 2021, May 28, 2023 and May 22, 2025.

ATPE, the Association of Texas Professional Educators, a teacher association, supported HB 6. Its Teach the Vote site describes HB 6 as a bill that "provides teachers and administrators with more tools to handle student discipline".

On April 6, 2023, she co-signed and voted for the $10,000 teacher-raise amendment to SB 9, the 2023 bill on educator rights, certification and pay, the Senate Journal records. She also voted for Nathan Johnson's amendment to keep the State Board of Education's power to reject educator-certification rules, and both amendments failed, the journal shows.

ATPE records that she voted for SB 798 of 2023, on ending the classroom-experience requirement for school counselors, and HB 1468 of 2021, on virtual schools. ATPE opposed both. ATPE also records that she voted against two 2021 charter-school bills, SB 28 and HB 3610. We did not check the journal for these votes.

She did not answer ATPE's 2022 or 2024 surveys, as Teach the Vote records.

Statewide executive offices

Benjamin Flores, Land Commissioner-elect

Elected November 3, 2026, over the incumbent, Republican Dawn Buckingham. The Associated Press called the race. The returns are unofficial and not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Flores has pledged to protect the Permanent School Fund from voucher programs and to send more state land revenue to public schools.

The land commissioner chairs the School Land Board, which oversees the lands of the Permanent School Fund, a state fund for public schools. The commissioner also holds one of nine seats on the board of the corporation that manages the fund's investments.

Flores has held no state office, and we found no vote by him on a school matter. His campaign Q&A pledges to protect the fund from being "raided for voucher schemes" and names raising its revenue his top priority.

We found no statement on teacher preparation or certification.

Background and powers of the office

Flores has held no state office. He has sat on the Bay City City Council since 2023, a city posting shows. He works as a cybersecurity and compliance consultant, his campaign biography says.

His 2023 council-campaign site, in a copy archived May 12, 2024, says he was president of the parent association at Holy Cross Catholic School in Bay City, the private school his daughter attends.

Two accounts of his move to Bay City differ. His campaign biography says the family moved from Austin to Bay City in 2016. His city biography says they moved to Austin in 2016 and to Bay City several years later.

The land commissioner's education duties concern the Permanent School Fund, a state fund for public schools. The commissioner heads the General Land Office, or GLO, and chairs the School Land Board, under Natural Resources Code §32.014. That board oversees the fund's lands. The fund includes "all income from the mineral development of permanent school fund land," under Education Code §43.001.

The commissioner also holds one of nine seats on the board of the Texas Permanent School Fund Corporation, which has managed the fund's investments since 2021, under Education Code §43.053.

State guarantees of charter-school bonds are approved by the commissioner of education, not the land commissioner, under Education Code §45.052. We found no GLO power over charter schools.

The same Q&A page names "Permanent School Fund Optimization" his top priority and says it "could generate up to $825 million more annually for Texas public schools, potentially lowering everyone's property taxes". His home page pledges to expand oil, gas, wind, solar and geothermal leasing "to increase revenue benefiting the Permanent School Fund." In the League of Women Voters Houston voters guide, he wrote: "I'll responsibly lease state land for every dollar it can honestly return, publish what each acre earns, and send more of it to classrooms."

Statewide executive offices

Clayton Tucker, Agriculture Commissioner-elect

Elected November 3, 2026, over Republican Nate Sheets in an open seat. Sheets had defeated the incumbent, Sid Miller, in the Republican primary. The Associated Press called the race, and the returns are unofficial and not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Most of Tucker's 2026 pledges concern school meals, including free meals for all children and food from Texas farmers in public schools.

The agriculture commissioner runs the Texas Department of Agriculture, which by law administers the school lunch, school breakfast and summer food service programs.

Tucker has held no public office, and his campaign's meals page pledges free meals for all children and rules requiring all school food to come from Texas farmers. His October 19, 2026 newsletter put the local-food pledge differently.

In 2023 a statement of the Texas Progressive Caucus, which he then led, warned Democratic lawmakers against any voucher deal. On teacher preparation, we found only one 2020 campaign line.

Background and powers of the office

Tucker has held no public office and lost a 2020 race for Texas Senate District 24 to Dawn Buckingham. He also lost a 2021 Lampasas city-council race.

His campaign biography describes him as a rancher near Lampasas and a former kindergarten teacher in Taipei. The Texas Farmers Union, a farm organization, lists him as its current secretary on its officers page. In 2023 he was president of the Texas Progressive Caucus, a progressive political organization, a caucus statement shows.

The agriculture commissioner's education duties described here concern school meals. The commissioner runs the Texas Department of Agriculture, or TDA, which "shall administer" the school lunch, school breakfast and summer food service programs, among others, under Agriculture Code §12.0025. Section 12.0026 of the same chapter sets up a farm-to-school task force on "locally grown food products in public schools."

TDA says the school lunch program serves "more than 3 million Texas children". Summer EBT, also called SUN Bucks, is not a TDA program: the Texas Tribune reported "a $60 million addition for the Texas Health and Human Services Commission to administer such a program."

Statewide executive offices

Jon Rosenthal, Railroad Commissioner-elect

Rosenthal was elected November 3, 2026, over Republican Bo French in an open seat. The race was called by the Associated Press. The results are unofficial and not certified. The state canvass, the official count, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Rosenthal voted against the 2025 education savings account law at both House readings and wrote in 2020 that he would support no voucher program.

The Railroad Commission regulates oil and gas wells and pipelines. We found no statute giving it authority over schools. Oil and gas production taxes reach schools through the comptroller, not the commission.

In the House, he voted no on Senate Bill 2 of 2025 at second and third reading. The bill created state-funded education savings accounts for private schooling. In a 2020 survey he called the state's standardized tests "detrimental to the point of being criminal".

He voted for House Bill 2 of 2025, on school finance and teacher pay, at second and third reading, then against the final version. He voted against House Bill 8, the 2025 testing law, at all three recorded stages, and we found no explanation from him of these votes.

We found no pledge, statement or post on teacher preparation or certification. His record on it is bills, chiefly one he filed in four sessions on assigning students to uncertified teachers, first in 2019.

Background and powers of the office

Rosenthal has represented Texas House District 135, in northwest Harris County, since January 2019, the Legislative Reference Library records. His campaign site and Community Impact say he was first elected in 2018 over the Republican incumbent, Gary Elkins.

He is a mechanical engineer with 25 years in oil and gas, Texas Public Radio says. He did not seek re-election to the House in order to run for the Railroad Commission, the same report says.

His member pages for 2019, 2021, 2023 and 2025 list assignments that included Energy Resources, County Affairs, and Agriculture and Livestock, but never the House Public Education or Higher Education committees.

The Railroad Commission of Texas regulates oil and gas wells and pipelines, under Natural Resources Code §81.051. We found no statute giving the commission authority over schools.

Oil and gas production taxes reach schools through the comptroller, not the commission, under Tax Code §202.353 and §201.404. After other deductions, the comptroller deposits "one-fourth of the revenue collected from the tax imposed by this chapter to the credit of the foundation school fund". The foundation school fund is a state fund for public schools.

Record by issue

General notes

Campaign pledge

His 2020 pledges are written answers to a survey by the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association that does not endorse candidates. ATPE published them on its Teach the Vote site. He did not answer its 2022 or 2024 surveys, the site shows.

Social media

We searched all 121 original posts on his Bluesky account, jon-rosenthaltx.bsky.social. We did not fetch his X, Facebook, Instagram, Threads or YouTube accounts. One post, on July 27, 2026, says "my opponent is attacking Texas seniors, students, and neighbors with disabilities". The post states no education policy.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Private-school vouchers and education savings accounts. Asked whether he would support any voucher, education savings account or tax-credit program, he answered in the 2020 survey: "No. Nope. No way." An education savings account is a state-funded account that parents can spend on private schooling.

Statement or interview

Private-school vouchers and education savings accounts. His statements from 2023 and 2025 oppose vouchers. On October 12, 2023, he said, as quoted by the Houston Chronicle: "Vouchers are a scam that take money out of our schools."

The Chronicle reported his view that the money "would be better used to increase the basic allotment and give raises to teachers". The basic allotment is the base per-student amount in the state formula.

On April 2, 2025, he told the Houston Chronicle about Senate Bill 2 of 2025, which created education savings accounts: "It's not a school choice package at all, it's a discount for kids who are already in private schools."

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

His pledges on funding and pay come from election night in 2018 and the 2020 survey. On election night in 2018 he told Community Impact: "We're going to address education first and health care second."

In the 2020 survey he wrote "Keep the defined benefit pension plan for sure," about the teacher retirement system. In the same survey he wrote: "Teacher pay should be determined on multiple criteria (certainly including seniority!)."

Statement or interview

His statements from 2019 and 2024 ask for more state funding for schools and raises for educators.

  • Community Impact reported on June 26, 2019 that "he would like to see more comprehensive school system funding to provide more raises to educators."
  • The Houston Chronicle reported that he spoke on May 6, 2024, at a board meeting of Cypress-Fairbanks ISD, the Cypress-Fairbanks Independent School District, on budget and librarian cuts. It wrote that he was "asking every Texan watching to call their representatives and ask for increased funding to public education."
  • The same report says he was one of six area House members who signed a letter "urging the Texas Education Agency to release the $30 million from the TEA's surplus". Republican Rep. Tom Oliverson led the bipartisan group.
  • On May 13, 2024, he and about 40 lawmakers asked Gov. Greg Abbott for a special session. Their letter said: "These issues arise from the state's failure to improve school funding since 2019". The passage appears in Spectrum News. Abbott replied that the signers had voted against a school-funding bill tied to vouchers, according to ABC13.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

His 2020 survey answers call for replacing the state tests. In the 2020 survey he called STAAR, the state's standardized tests, "detrimental to the point of being criminal" and set a goal to "repeal and replace" them.

He wrote: "First steps are to decouple it from school accountability and also further increase pilot programs for alternative testing and evaluation systems." For low-rated schools he wrote: "How about instead we allocate EXTRA resources to struggling schools".

Statement or interview

On August 13, 2025, he told the Houston Press, "I'm an anti-STAAR crusader," and said he wanted to "revise or actually kill the STAAR test."

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

In the 2020 survey he wrote that "not all charter operations are inherently evil" but that "With today's current budget crunch there is NO WAY that any new charters should be approved."

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Statement or interview

On June 17, 2024, after the Cypress-Fairbanks ISD board removed science-textbook chapters on vaccines, climate change and cultural diversity, he said in the Houston Chronicle: "As a science-based career professional and a state rep who values and supports public education I'm appalled".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

His 2026 campaign priority page pledges to "partner with local business and community colleges on paid training."

Statement or interview

During House debate on Senate Bill 18 of 2023, on faculty tenure, he said: "My family came to Texas because of the tenure program at The University of Texas." The House Journal records the remark on May 22, 2023.

Other

Statement or interview

Other: oil and gas revenue. He told KTAB on July 26, 2026: "The revenues that come from oil and gas production pay for our schools, our roads, our parks, and so much more."

65 rows

How a teacher association describes some of these votes. ATPE's profile lists several of his votes that went against the association's positions. According to ATPE's Teach the Vote profile, he voted for two 2021 bills expanding full-time virtual schools, House Bill 1468 and Senate Bill 15, which ATPE opposed.

ATPE records that he voted against the 2023 school-safety conference report and the 2025 discipline bill, House Bill 6, which ATPE supported. ATPE opposed Senate Bill 9 of 2023, for which he voted, "as insufficient in terms of providing a meaningful increase in educator compensation", Teach the Vote says.

ATPE also reports a vote on House Bill 547 of 2021, on home-schooled students' participation in public-school activities. He was recorded as voting yes on concurrence but entered a statement that he intended to vote no, ATPE says.

Bills he authored on education.

  • Teacher preparation and certification. He filed the same bill in four sessions, each on the assignment of students to uncertified teachers. It was House Bill 1276, or HB 1276, in 2019, then HB 800 in 2021, HB 1005 in 2023 and HB 362 in 2025. The 2019 text said that in districts of at least 5,000 students, a student in grades 1 to 6 "may not be assigned for two consecutive school years to a teacher who" has less than one year of experience and lacks the required certificate. Parents could consent to the assignment. The 2019 bill passed the House on April 25, 2019 and did not pass the Senate, according to Teach the Vote. He was also a joint author of HB 116 of 2019, on educator training, and a coauthor of HB 1569 of 2023, on training computer-science teachers.
  • Testing, accountability and state takeovers. His bills would have changed how the state takes over school districts and how state tests count in school ratings. HB 3545 of 2019 would have replaced a state-appointed board of managers with a "community management board" including "a classroom teacher from the school district or campus." HB 3071 of 2021, filed with Rep. Garnet Coleman, said "the commissioner may not order the appointment of a board of managers to govern a school district unless at least 15 percent of the campuses" were rated unacceptable. HB 2661 of 2023 would have ended the use of state tests as indicators of achievement in school ratings.
  • Charter schools. HB 1320 of 2021, refiled in 2023 and 2025, would have applied state travel-expense rules to charter schools spending state money. It never passed.
  • School funding and teacher pay. HB 3380 of 2025 would have raised the basic allotment from $6,160 to "the lesser of $7,500" or a formula amount, with an inflation adjustment. He was a coauthor of HB 3 of 2019, the school-finance law.
  • Higher education. HB 626 of 2021, which became law, expanded an adult career-education grant program.

Education-oriented backers

  • Texas AFT COPE endorsed him on its May 26 and October 1, 2026 lists. Texas AFT COPE is the political committee of Texas AFT, the Texas affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers. He is not on the 2026 list of the Texas State Teachers Association, or TSTA, and we found no 2026 teacher-organization money.
  • In his earlier House races, TSTA's 2024 list includes him. A campaign-finance report lists $500 from its political committee on November 18, 2024, after that general election. In 2018, in Community Impact, he credited "backing from the Cy-Fair branch of the American Federation of Teachers". Teach the Vote says he was "Endorsed in the 2022 general election by Texas Parent PAC," a parent political committee.
  • We found no charter or school-choice backing. For his opponent, the Texas Home School Coalition endorsed French on its endorsement list.

What was not found

  • Teacher preparation and certification. We found no pledge, statement or post. His record on this subject is the bills above.
  • We found no personal explanation of his votes against the final versions of House Bill 2 and House Bill 8 of 2025, and no statement on the state's takeover of Houston ISD.
  • We could not confirm two reported items: two 2021 letters on virtual instruction and STAAR that he is said to have signed, and scorecards from Young Conservatives of Texas and another group marking him against their school-choice positions.

Texas Legislature

The Texas Legislature after the 2026 election

Democrats are projected to control the Texas House and Republicans the Texas Senate, so neither party holds both chambers of the Legislature. In the 150-member House, the MultiState tracker counted 81 Democrats and 64 Republicans as of November 9, 2026, with five seats last held by Republicans not yet called. If current leads hold, the House will be 83 Democrats to 67 Republicans.

The 31-member Senate is projected at 19 Republicans to 12 Democrats, as the Texas Tribune reported on November 5, 2026, and, according to Texas Public Radio, in Patrick's words on November 9. The Texan reported that Republicans hold 20 seats. No legislative result is certified, and the state canvass, the official count, ends by December 7, 2026, under a Secretary of State advisory.

The Legislature writes the state's education laws and its two-year budget. The Senate also confirms the governor's appointees, including the commissioner of education, under §7.051 of the Education Code.

The 2027 regular session opens January 12, 2027, under Government Code §301.001. The constitution limits it to 140 days, so its last day is May 31, 2027. Legislators and legislators-elect can file bills from November 9, 2026, until March 12, 2027, the Texas Municipal League reported.

Hinojosa takes office as governor on January 19, 2027, under article IV, section 4 of the constitution, a date FOX 26 also gives.

The table shows the votes each action takes and whether either party can take it alone on projected results. The Senate's regular order of business is its procedure for taking up bills, and setting it aside to take up a bill takes five-ninths of those present, under its vote chart.

ActionRuleVotes neededWho can do it alone
House: pass a billmajority (Texas Tribune)a majority of those voting, 76 if all 150 voteDemocrats
House: elect a Speakermajority (Texas Tribune)a majority of those voting, 76 if all 150 voteDemocrats
Senate: take up a bill out of the regular order of businessfive-ninths of those present (Senate vote chart)18 of 31Republicans
Senate: change the Senate's rulesmajority of all members (Senate Rules)16 of 31Republicans
Senate: confirm an appointeetwo-thirds of those present (constitution)21 of 31neither party
Override a vetotwo-thirds of the members present in the chamber where the bill began, then two-thirds of the members of the other chamber (constitution, article IV, section 14)100 in the House and 21 in the Senate when all attendneither party
Quorum to do business"Two-thirds of each House shall constitute a quorum to do business" (constitution, article III, section 10)100 of 150 in the House and 21 of 31 in the Senateneither party

The quorum rule in the constitution means the minority party in either chamber can stop business by staying away. For a veto override, the constitution requires that "two-thirds of the members present agree to pass the bill" in the first chamber. In the second, it must be "approved by two-thirds of the members of that House".

Sarah Eckhardt's and Nathan Johnson's Senate seats become vacant when they take statewide office, until special elections that the Austin American-Statesman reports have not been called. Confirmation would then take 20 of 29 senators if all attend.

The Legislature last overrode a veto in 1979, on a bill under Governor William P. Clements Jr., the Legislative Reference Library lists.

The lieutenant governor, who presides over the Senate, appoints its committees and refers its bills under the Senate's rules. The Senate adopts its rules at the start of the session, which opens January 12, 2027, and a majority of 16 senators can take those powers away. Her deciding vote in a tie comes from the constitution and cannot be removed that way.

Dan Patrick, the outgoing lieutenant governor, urged Republican senators on November 9 to take those powers from Goodwin. Republican senators have been meeting privately to discuss it, the Statesman reported, but no resolution has been filed. We found no sitting Republican senator backing a specific change, and Senator Paul Bettencourt said the decision is up to the Senate, the Dallas Morning News reported.

Goodwin said she hopes for "a collaborative environment in the Senate," the Statesman reported.

North Carolina's Democrat-controlled Senate took such powers from the lieutenant governor in 1989. The Texas Senate did not in 1997 and 1998, when its majority and Lieutenant Governor Bob Bullock, a Democrat, were of different parties, the Statesman reported. Our estimate of this change is in the sections "Implications for the future" and "How we made the estimates", the only parts of this document that look ahead.

The House elects its Speaker by a majority on January 12, 2027, and the Speaker presides and appoints committee chairs. Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat, is the leading candidate. Eddie Morales Jr. withdrew and endorsed her on November 6, and she released a list of 90 supporters, eight of them Republicans, the Texas Tribune reported.

She said she would appoint members of both parties to chair committees, the same article reported, and the Republican caucus has not chosen a nominee.

U.S. Senate

James Talarico, U.S. senator-elect

Result: the Associated Press called the race for Talarico over Ken Paxton, a Republican, as shown in the Texas Tribune's live results, which use Associated Press data. His margin is 1,195,609 votes in the Texas Secretary of State's unofficial count. The result is not certified. The state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Talarico, a House Public Education Committee member from 2019 through 2025, voted against the 2025 education savings account law in committee and on the floor.

A senator's education powers are federal. Senators vote on appropriations for the U.S. Department of Education and confirm its Secretary. The office has no direct authority over Texas teacher certification or state school-finance formulas.

He voted no on Senate Bill 2 of 2025, which created state-funded education savings accounts for private schooling, in committee and at second and third reading. Every statement we found from 2023 to 2026 opposes vouchers. He has also written that high-quality nonprofit public charter schools have a role in the education system.

His account of once having 45 students in one classroom is disputed. The Daily Wire reported, citing a New York Times profile we could not open, that his largest class had 30 students. His campaign says 45 were placed in his classroom before students were redistributed.

His only pledge on educator preparation is to expand federal programs such as the Teacher Quality Partnership. We found no statement from him on teacher residencies or alternative certification.

Background and powers of the office

Talarico taught sixth-grade language arts at Rhodes Middle School in San Antonio ISD from 2011 to 2013. He taught as a Teach For America corps member and then spent a year at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. The Texas Tribune gives these details in an article of January 16, 2026. ISD stands for independent school district.

By 2016 he was Central Texas executive director of Reasoning Mind, a nonprofit offering computer-based math instruction. The San Antonio Report gives that title. The Legislative Reference Library records that he won a special election to the Texas House on November 6, 2018.

His page on Teach the Vote lists him as the member for House District 52, then District 50 after his 2022 reelection. That site belongs to the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association that does not endorse candidates. From 2019 to 2025 he also worked for Maya Consulting LLC, an education consulting firm. His Senate financial disclosure lists $83,333.40 paid to him by the firm in 2025.

The committee roster shows him on the House Public Education Committee in all four regular sessions from 2019 through 2025. His member page shows that in 2023 he also sat on the select committee that took up vouchers. In 2025 he was vice chair of a Public Education subcommittee on academic and career education, the page shows.

The same page lists his service on two House-Senate conference committees in 2023. One was on school chaplains, Senate Bill 763, or SB 763. The other was on pre-kindergarten teacher requirements, House Bill 2729, or HB 2729.

A senator's education powers are federal. Senators vote on the appropriations that fund the U.S. Department of Education. The U.S. Constitution says "No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law".

Senators also give "Advice and Consent" on officers of the United States, among them the Secretary of Education, under the Constitution. The office has no direct authority over Texas teacher certification, state school-finance formulas or the Texas Education Agency, the state agency that oversees public schools. We found no Senate committee assignment for him.

Record by issue

General notes

Campaign pledge

The pledges below come from his campaign's public-education page unless another source is named. The page was published January 2, 2026, and modified October 12, 2026.

Statement or interview

Quotations are his own words unless marked as campaign or reporter text.

Social media

All the posts we found are on X. We checked his X account, @jamestalarico, through posts embedded on his campaign pages and through Thread Reader. We did not retrieve his Instagram, TikTok, Facebook or YouTube accounts, and we did not check Bluesky or Threads. The posts:

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

His campaign pages pledge to oppose vouchers. The public-education page pledges to "Reject the voucher scams being pushed by billionaire mega-donors that defund public schools to subsidize private education for the wealthiest Americans". His rural-investment page pledges to "Oppose the federal voucher scam being pushed by billionaires like Betsy DeVos," without naming a federal bill.

Statement or interview

Every statement we found from 2023 to 2026 opposes private-school vouchers.

  • On April 7, 2023, after the House barred state budget money for vouchers, his office issued a release, reprinted by the Gilmer Mirror: "They have a simple strategy: First, demonize, and then dismantle public education".
  • In July 2023, he spoke at the House select committee's hearing, as reported by ATPE. He said: "It’s my opinion we shouldn’t be messing with any pet projects or education savings accounts until we do the $1,000 increase." He also asked the Texas Education Agency what federal protections special-education students give up by taking an education savings account. An education savings account is a state-funded account parents can spend on private schooling.
  • In his 2024 ATPE candidate survey, he wrote on Teach the Vote: "No. I am against voucher scams in any shape or size and will never vote to defund our public schools".
  • On April 16, 2025, the House debated SB 2, the bill that created the state's education savings accounts. He said: "This amendment would send this private school voucher bill to the voters of Texas for their approval before it can be implemented." He gave the reason that "private schools can deny admission to any kid for any reason they want." The House tabled the amendment, the House Journal records.
  • At a primary debate on January 24, 2026, he said, in the Texas Tribune: "I have gone toe to toe with the billionaires who are trying to dismantle public education in this state".

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

His statements on funding and pay call for full funding of the Department of Education and a raise for educators. At a CNN town hall on October 14, 2026, he said, "One, I would make sure that we fully fund the Department of Education." He also said: "I think we can do so much to finally pass a pay raise for our hardworking educators." He named no federal mechanism for the raise.

KLTV reported on May 29, 2026 that "he hopes to push at the federal level to incentivize states to get teachers above the national average".

Statement or interview

School funding, teacher pay and class size. He voted for the 2025 school-finance law while calling it inadequate, and he has said that an education system built on property wealth is unequal. On April 16, 2025, the House Journal records him speaking about HB 2, the 2025 school-finance and teacher-pay law. He said: "I voted for that bill in committee and on the floor, but I also made the point on this back microphone that it was inadequate to the crisis that our schools are facing".

Explaining why he left teaching, he told the Tribune: "An education system that is built on property wealth is always going to be inherently unequal". At the CNN town hall, he said: "I believe that educators should be sitting at the decision-making table when it comes to making decisions about education policy".

His campaign site says he "Overhauled Texas’s school finance system and invested over $6.5 billion into public schools for teacher pay raises, educator training, new literacy and math proficiency initiatives", on the public-education page. The bill history of that 2019 law, HB 3, lists him as one of about 140 coauthors, not one of its five authors. In 2024 he wrote on Teach the Vote that "crafting HB 3 and fixing our broken school finance system, was my top priority".

Two accounts of his class size exist. He has said he had 45 students in one classroom, on his campaign page and at the CNN town hall: "At one point, I had 45 students in one classroom".

The Daily Wire, a conservative outlet, reported on October 28, 2026, citing a New York Times profile, that "Texas Education Agency documents reviewed by the Times, however, indicate that the largest class period he taught at Rhodes Middle School had 30 students, while most of his classes ranged from 22 to 27". The same article quotes campaign spokesman JT Ennis: "After having 45 students placed in his classroom, James worked with school administrators to redistribute students across classes and create the learning environment that his students deserved".

We could not open the New York Times profile that the Daily Wire cites, so the class-size figure is reported here secondhand.

Social media

  • On May 14, 2021, he posted: "I just passed legislation to limit the size of pre-k classes to 22 students in Texas". On January 24, 2023, he posted: "Today I’m introducing legislation to give every teacher in Texas a $15,000 pay raise".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing and instruction. His one pledge here is for grants "to encourage public schools to adopt evidence-based strategies like phonics, early literacy programs, and 1:1 intensive tutoring", on the public-education page. He made no pledge on charter schools.

Statement or interview

In his 2022 and 2024 surveys on Teach the Vote, he wrote that tests should not be "the sole, or even the majority, means of evaluating teachers". He also wrote that "the current testing regime represents an overcorrection and must be addressed".

On July 13, 2026, he spoke about the state takeover of Houston ISD and about vouchers in Texas Metro News. He said: "There is a coordinated effort by some of the most powerful politicians, and some of the wealthiest mega donors to dismantle public education".

Charter schools

Statement or interview

He supports nonprofit public charters as public-school choice. In 2022 he wrote on Teach the Vote: "I believe there is a role for high-quality nonprofit public charter schools in our education system." He added that his concern is "not with the number of public charter schools, but with the quality".

On the House floor on April 16, 2025, he said, as the House Journal records: "we could open more magnets, more academies, more career and technical schools, more public charter schools, eliminate the wait-lists". He also said: "I'm talking about real school choice, which I support and have supported since I got to this body".

Seth Rau, who wrote his 2018 education platform, wrote in SCHOOLED on March 10, 2026 that Talarico "has been very close to the leaders of the Texas charter school movement, and they hosted many of his earliest fundraisers during his 2018 campaign".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum and religion in schools. His freedom-family-faith page pledges to "reject policies that force religion into neutral public spaces like schools, prisons, courts, and the military".

Statement or interview

His statements and amendments concern race in the curriculum, the Ten Commandments bills, school chaplains and Bluebonnet Learning.

  • On May 28, 2021, on HB 3979, the 2021 bill limiting how teachers address race, he asked: "Is it fair to say that any bill that strikes language condemning racism is a racist bill?" The question appears in a Texas Tribune article carried by Click2Houston. An ATPE blog post records that his point of order against the Senate's amendments was sustained.
  • On May 2, 2023, at a committee hearing on SB 1515, a Senate bill requiring Ten Commandments displays, he said, in remarks carried by KUTV: "This bill to me is not only unconstitutional, it's not only un-American, I think it is also deeply un-Christian".
  • On May 8, 2023, on SB 763, the school chaplains bill, the House adopted his amendment requiring chaplains to be endorsed by an organization the Department of Defense recognizes. His amendment requiring parental consent before a child meets a chaplain failed, 61 to 76, the House Journal records.
  • In 2024 he questioned Commissioner Mike Morath about Bluebonnet Learning, the state-written materials that HB 1605 of 2023 led to. He asked: "How do you believe teachers will respond to elementary school students when they ask how a human being can rise from the dead?" The question appears in The 74.
  • In 2025 he spoke about the Ten Commandments law, SB 10. He said: "I worry that these kinds of bills will actually create a new generation of atheists who think our religion is more about power than love." The Austin Chronicle places this in an April debate with Rep. Candy Noble. Texas Public Radio describes a similar argument in the May 24 floor debate, where he said, "The separation of church and state doesn't just protect the state. It also protects the church".

Social media

  • Curriculum and religion. On May 28, 2021, he posted on HB 3979: "If kids are old enough to experience racism, then they're old enough to learn about it", in a thread on Thread Reader. On May 3, 2023, he posted: "This bill is not only un-constitutional and un-American, it’s deeply un-Christian". A March 1, 2024 post embedded on his faith page reads: "The 25 largest school districts in Texas all rejected replacing counselors with chaplains". A May 29, 2025 post embedded on the same page reads: "forcing teachers to post the Ten Commandments violates the most important commandment: love thy neighbor".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

His only pledge on educator preparation is on the public-education page. It reads: "Hire more teachers and equip them with what they need to succeed: Expand programs like the Teacher Quality Partnership, the Supporting Effective Educator Development program, and the TEACH grant that fund and enhance teacher training and are helping to close the teacher workforce gap". The pledge gives no dollar amounts and does not mention residencies or alternative certification.

Statement or interview

He entered teaching through Teach For America after graduating from the University of Texas. The sources differ on his graduation year: 2011 according to the Daily Texan and 2010 according to the Texas Tribune.

The Tribune gives his teaching years as 2011 to 2013. We did not find which certification program he completed or what his certificate type is.

  • His one located answer on the supply of certified teachers is in his 2024 survey on Teach the Vote. He wrote: "the best way to have adequate numbers of trained and certified teachers is to listen to Governor Abbott's own Teacher Vacancy Task Force which recommended increasing teacher pay." He also named retirement benefits and workload. The answer addresses pay, not preparation or certification routes.
  • On August 13, 2024, the House Public Education Committee held an interim hearing on teacher certification. The Texas Classroom Teachers Association, or TCTA, a teacher association, reported that he "asked for more details about the survey", meaning TCTA's member survey on uncertified teachers. TCTA named him among members "particularly supportive of teachers and the teaching profession throughout the hearing." We found no quotation of his own words on certification from the hearing.
  • A machine transcript of the Joe Rogan podcast of July 18, 2025, is on Rosetta. It has him saying high-poverty schools give "the kids who have the most troubles to the first year teachers … Almost like a hazing thing".
  • His educator-workforce bills are under "Voting record." They are the 2021 law changing the composition of the State Board for Educator Certification, which sets certification rules, and a 2025 bill on teachers' appeals under the state's teacher-designation pay system. His votes on certification and counselor bills are there too.
  • Rep. Carl Tepper, a Republican, said in the Texas Tribune that he "should never claim to be an expert in education because of two years in the classroom".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

His higher-education pledges concern career programs and federal student aid. The public-education page pledges to improve "junior college and Career and Technical Education programs".

The Texas Tribune covered his positions in an article carried by KSAT on October 8, 2026. It wrote that he "has called for a reversal of federal cuts to the U.S Department of Education and for additional funding for Pell Grants and other student aid". FOX 7 Austin drew on the campaign and his legislative remarks in an article of October 21, 2026. It wrote that he "advocated for expanding the value of federal Pell Grants, indexing them to inflation" and "supports student debt relief".

Statement or interview

We found no statement naming SB 17 of 2023 or SB 37 of 2025, the laws on university diversity offices and university governance. His votes against both are under "Voting record."

Other

Campaign pledge

The public-education page also pledges universal pre-kindergarten "for every 3- and 4-year-old" and protection of "federal oversight that ensures special education students receive the funding and support they need". The same page pledges expansion of "the National School Lunch and School Breakfast programs," more school counselors, and federal guidelines "that can help states and schools safely use AI in the classroom".

Statement or interview

He called HB 3 of 2023, which required an armed security officer at each campus, "another unfunded mandate on public schools", on Teach the Vote.

On September 9, 2026, he said, "I will oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it risks safety or fairness." The Texas Tribune's headline calls this a reversal. In 2021 he voted against HB 25, which limited school sports teams by biological sex, the House Journal records.

His campaign page and a 2023 post on X say he put Narcan, a drug that reverses opioid overdoses, "on EVERY school campus". The law he sponsored, SB 629 of 2023, requires an opioid-antagonist policy "at each campus in the district that serves students in grades 6 through 12", as its enrolled text shows.

Social media

  • On May 26, 2023, he posted: "I just passed a bill to put Narcan on EVERY school campus in Texas".

The Houston Chronicle reported on October 20, 2026 that Reed Hastings gave $1,000,000 to outside groups supporting Talarico, not to his campaign. The Chronicle did not name the receiving committee.

The Texas Tribune reported on May 14, 2026 that Stephen Mandel, a Teach For America board member, gave $500,000 to Lone Star Rising PAC, a super PAC supporting him that operates independently of his campaign.

Other education-oriented backers. His reports list $5,000 from Charles Butt, as an individual, on October 24, 2018 and $5,000 on October 31, 2018. An independent expenditure is spending by an outside group that is not coordinated with the campaign. We found no independent expenditure by the NEA Advocacy Fund, AFT Solidarity or Democrats for Education Reform among 278 federal filings naming him. The filings run from January 13 to September 30, 2026, and we did not check October filings. Backing for the opponent: the Texas Home School Coalition endorsed Ken Paxton.

What was not found

  • We searched without result for questionnaire answers to Raise Your Hand Texas, TSTA or Texas AFT, and for education remarks from a general-election debate. We found no positions on Title I amounts, a federal special-education funding target, the federal tax-credit scholarship law by name or federal graduate-loan limits. Title I is the federal aid program for schools with many low-income students.
  • We found no statements on teacher residencies, alternative-certification providers, online educator preparation, certification-board rules or the certification provisions of HB 2 of 2025. We also found no statement offering an alternative to the Houston ISD takeover and no statement naming SB 17 or SB 37.
  • We did not search or could not read his teaching-certificate record and his 2018 and 2020 campaign platforms.
  • We could not confirm a Texas Observer essay of April 2026 on campaign money from Leadership for Educational Equity and a five-week Teach For America summer institute, because its page was blocked. We could not confirm a reported August 2024 hearing remark on training teachers in classroom management, because the cited page did not load. Nor could we confirm an Axios report of a remark about him by Governor Abbott, TikTok view counts for his 2023 Ten Commandments video, or contributions from John and Laura Arnold.

Texas Supreme Court

The Texas Supreme Court and public schools

The four Democratic wins in 2026 "will leave the GOP with a 5-4 advantage on the Supreme Court," in the Texas Tribune's words on November 4, 2026, with Maggie Ellis as chief justice. The Texas Supreme Court is the state's highest court for civil cases. Before the election, "All of the current justices are Republicans," the Texas Tribune's guide to the races says.

The justices "get to decide which cases to review, and their rulings … are final," the same guide says.

School cases reach the court from the intermediate courts of appeals, the appeals courts that sit below it. The dockets in this section show these kinds of school cases:

  • suits against the Texas Education Agency, the commissioner of education and the State Board for Educator Certification, which licenses and disciplines educators
  • state takeovers of districts
  • teacher contracts and pay grievances
  • school finance
  • immunity defenses of districts and charter schools

Until 2024, most suits against state agencies went on appeal to the Third Court of Appeals in Austin. Ellis, Chari Kelly and Gisela Triana sit on that court. Senate Bill 1045 of 2023 shifted that role. It created a Fifteenth Court of Appeals with "exclusive intermediate appellate jurisdiction" over cases brought by or against state agencies.

The law applies to appeals perfected on or after September 1, 2024. On that date it moved to the new court the pending cases of that kind in other courts of appeals that had been filed on or after September 1, 2023. Cases filed earlier stayed in the Third Court.

We found no statement by any of the four winners on vouchers, school finance, testing or the state takeover of the Houston Independent School District. The rules for judges limit what candidates for the court may say. Canon 5(1) of the Code of Judicial Conduct says: "A judge or judicial candidate shall not: (i) make pledges or promises of conduct in office regarding pending or impending cases, specific classes of cases, specific classes of litigants, or specific propositions of law that would suggest to a reasonable person that the judge is predisposed to a probable decision in cases within the scope of the pledge." Canon 3B(10) applies a similar limit on public comment about pending cases to candidates.

As of November 9, 2026, these education cases were pending at the court or could reach it. Two had been argued and were undecided.

  • Morath v. Texas State Teachers Association, No. 25-0527. The case challenges the commissioner's rule for district campuses run by outside partners under Senate Bill 1882 of 2017. The court granted review on June 12, 2026, and heard argument on October 7, 2026, the docket shows. It has not ruled. Ellis joined the Third Court opinion under review.
  • Texas Public Policy Foundation v. Highland Park ISD, No. 25-0759. The question is whether an exception in the Public Information Act covers attorney-client material, here a school district's investigation report. The act is the state law that requires government bodies to disclose information on request. The court heard argument on October 8, 2026, and has not ruled, the docket shows.
  • Harris County Department of Education Public Facility Corp. v. Paradigm Construction, No. 26-0790. This governmental-immunity dispute over a construction contract comes from Kristen Hawkins's district court. Governmental immunity is the rule that protects government bodies from some lawsuits. The case is at the petition stage, and the court ordered a response by November 2, 2026. On October 14, 2026, it granted in part a motion to extend that deadline and set the response as due December 2, 2026, the docket shows.
  • Excellence 2000 Inc. v. Texas Education Agency, No. 26-1213. The petition was filed October 22, 2026, and is under review, the docket shows. We did not read its subject.
  • In re Midland ISD, No. 26-0867. The court denied an emergency mandamus petition by the Midland school district against the commissioner of education on August 12, 2026, the docket shows. A mandamus petition asks a higher court to order an official or a lower court to act or to undo an act.
  • School ratings. Two suits over A-F ratings, the state's letter grades for districts and schools, ended in the Fifteenth Court of Appeals in 2025. The dockets for Kingsville ISD and Pecos-Barstow-Toyah ISD show those outcomes. We found no Supreme Court petition.
  • We found no Texas Supreme Court case on the 2025 Ten Commandments law, which requires the Ten Commandments to be displayed in classrooms, or on the 2025 education savings account law, the state's voucher program.

Maggie Ellis, Chief Justice-elect, Supreme Court

Elected November 3, 2026, over the incumbent, Republican Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock. The Associated Press called the race. The posted results are unofficial and not certified. The canvass, the official count, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

We found one education ruling with Ellis on the panel, a 2025 decision on teachers' rights at partner-run campuses, now under Supreme Court review.

A Supreme Court justice votes on which cases the court takes and how it decides them.

On the Third Court of Appeals, Ellis joined a panel opinion holding that district-employed teachers at partner-run campuses keep their statutory rights. It struck two parts of the commissioner's rule and upheld three. The Supreme Court heard argument on October 7, 2026, and has not ruled.

The Houston Chronicle editorial board wrote that she and Blacklock "were circumspect about speaking directly to issues that may appear before them." We found no campaign pledge on education and no statement by her on teacher certification.

Background and powers of the office

Ellis has served on the Third Court of Appeals, an intermediate appeals court in Austin, since January 2025, the Tribune guide says. Her official biography says she was "elected to the Texas Third Court of Appeals in 2024".

Before that, she was an administrative law judge at the State Office of Administrative Hearings, a Travis County assistant district attorney and a lawyer in family, juvenile and child-welfare law, her biography says.

She told Spectrum News on December 10, 2019: "I graduated from UT with a degree in education, then I worked as a teacher." Her court biography lists her as PTA president and vice president in the Leander Independent School District, or Leander ISD, and as a member of a Leander ISD zoning board. Her campaign site says she is immediate past chair of the State Bar's Juvenile Law Section.

A Supreme Court justice votes on which cases the court takes and on how it decides them, as the Tribune guide explains.

We found no pledge on education. The Houston Chronicle editorial board interviewed her and Blacklock and wrote: "Both candidates were circumspect about speaking directly to issues that may appear before them."

Social media

Other

Statement or interview

Other: her teaching background. Her campaign presents her as a former teacher, and her campaign and court biographies describe her Leander ISD ties differently. Her campaign home page quotes her: "As a Justice on the Third Court of Appeals, a former teacher, foster mom, and PTA President, I have been a strong advocate for compassion and justice for our community."

The campaign biography says "she worked in public education through Leander ISD". Her court biography lists PTA and zoning-board roles there, not employment.

She told The Daily Texan on November 21, 2024: "It was really working with kids in the classroom that I knew something wasn't right at home."

Her court biography lists "federal education law" among the subjects of her hearings, trials and appeals. It names no case or client.

Chari Kelly, Justice-elect, Supreme Court Place 2

Elected November 3, 2026, over the incumbent, Republican Justice James P. Sullivan, who was appointed in 2025. The Associated Press called the race. The posted results are unofficial and not certified. The canvass, the official count, ends December 7, 2026.

In brief

Kelly wrote a 2022 opinion affirming an injunction for school districts against the governor's order barring local mask requirements, which the Supreme Court vacated.

Justices vote on which cases to take and how to decide them.

On the Third Court of Appeals, Kelly wrote the 2022 opinion on whether that order validly suspended the Education Code powers districts relied on to require masks. It affirmed the injunction for the districts and held "the Governor does not possess absolute authority under the Texas Disaster Act to preempt orders issued by governmental entities and officials". The Supreme Court vacated the judgment on June 30, 2023. Her campaign site republishes those words.

We found no campaign pledge on education. Her only certification rulings were two procedural dismissals in 2020, and we found no statement by her on teacher certification.

Teacher preparation and certification. Five of her rulings concern educator licensing. Three are trial-court reviews of SBEC certificate revocations, in the Gomez, Lange and Tran cases above. The other two are the A+ Texas Teachers order on the alternative-certification provider and her separate opinion in Caddo Mills.

In that concurrence, she wrote that "the school district's abrupt change in its course of dealing with an educator who had been employed by the district for 15 years in the same position, absent any cause, is the type of unfair surprise that borders on being unconscionable." State Board of Education

The State Board of Education and what it controls

The State Board of Education decides what Texas public-school students are taught and which teaching materials the state approves. It can also veto new charter schools and reject the rules that govern teacher certification. It is an elected board of 15 members, each "elected from districts", under Education Code §7.101. These are its powers, with the statute for each:

  • Curriculum standards. The board sets what each subject must teach. Under §28.002(c), it "shall by rule identify the essential knowledge and skills of each subject of the required curriculum". Texas calls these standards the TEKS, and §28.002(c) ties them to instructional materials and state tests. The board also sets graduation requirements, under §7.102(c)(4).
  • Instructional materials. Districts may not use materials the board rejects. The board reviews the materials sent to it by the Texas Education Agency, the state agency that runs public education, and keeps lists of approved and rejected materials, under §§31.022, 31.024.
  • Permanent School Fund. The board oversees the investment of the state's endowment for public schools. Section 43.003 says it "may invest the permanent school fund" under the Texas Constitution. Since a 2021 law, it has delegated day-to-day investment to the Texas Permanent School Fund Corporation. That corporation has a nine-member board, and five of its members are State Board members, under §§43.052, 43.053.
  • Charter veto. The board can veto a new charter school that the commissioner of education, who heads the Texas Education Agency, proposes. The charter takes effect unless, within 90 days, "a majority of the members of the board present and voting vote against the grant", under §12.101(b-0). The board may not vote on a charter the commissioner has not proposed.
  • Educator-certification rules. The board can reject, but not change, the rules for preparing and certifying teachers. Those rules come from the State Board for Educator Certification, a separate state board, which must send every rule it proposes to the State Board of Education. Under §21.042, the board "may reject a proposed rule by a vote of at least two-thirds of the members of the board present and voting" within 90 days but "may not modify" it. A rule it does not reject takes effect. The State Board of Education's review of the certification rules in June 2026 shows what those rules cover. The School Initiatives committee minutes of June 25, 2026 list admission to teacher-preparation programs, the programs themselves, certification exams and certificates.

The Texas Tribune voter guide of October 16, 2026 wrote that in 2026 the board passed "sweeping changes to social studies" for kindergarten through high school and "approved a new required reading list that includes Bible stories".

After the November 3, 2026 election, Democrats hold seven seats, Republicans hold seven, and the District 8 race is not called, as the Associated Press results on the Texas Tribune show. On the Secretary of State's results page, the results are unofficial until the state canvass, the official count, ends on December 7, 2026.

For most board decisions, the record does not show how each member voted. The board's minutes record most decisions only as "carried" or as a tally such as 8-7. A member's individual vote is on record for a minority of decisions. The vote tables below mark the rest "not recorded".

Thomas Ray Garcia, State Board of Education, District 2

Won a seat held by Republicans. The Associated Press called the race for Garcia over Republican Victoria Hinojosa, as the Texas Tribune's results page shows. The result is not certified.

In brief

Garcia, who has never held elected office, has a campaign platform against the state's voucher program and the state-written Bluebonnet Learning curriculum.

The seat is one of 15 on the State Board of Education, the elected board that sets curriculum standards. The board can reject, but not change, teacher-certification rules under Section 21.042.

His platform opposes the voucher program and Bluebonnet Learning, the state-written reading and math materials. His survey answer on Bluebonnet is narrower: it criticizes the materials but does not pledge to remove them.

He wrote that the board should be able to amend certification rules, which would take a change in the law. We found no statement on uncertified teachers, alternative certification or teacher residencies.

Background and powers of the office

Garcia teaches English at South Texas College, where he was an adjunct professor and professor in 2022-23 and again since 2024, as the Texas Tribune voter guide shows.

The same guide lists him as a teacher in the Pharr-San Juan-Alamo school district in 2016-17 and an instructor at UCLA in 2018-20. The guide also lists him as the founder and director of a college-access nonprofit, the College Scholarship Leadership Access Program, from 2013 to 2023.

He has held no elected office and ran unopposed in the March 2026 Democratic primary, as the primary results on Teach the Vote show. Teach the Vote is the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE.

The seat is one of the 15 on the State Board of Education, or SBOE, under Education Code §7.101. The board's powers are set out at the start of this section.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We checked his Bluesky account, thomasraygarcia.bsky.social, and read eight posts. We could not read his Facebook, Instagram or TikTok accounts without a login.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. His campaign platform page, undated and read November 9, 2026, says: "I am against our state's school voucher program." The page adds, "I support school choice in the form of open-enrollment public schools," and gives the reason: "The solution to improving our public schools is to invest more, not to defund them through voucher programs".

Social media

  • Vouchers and funding. On June 3, 2026, he posted on Bluesky: "At a time when public education is being underfunded and privatized, I couldn't stand aside".

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

His survey answer calls for doubling the state's base funding per student, and his platform supports higher pay for school workers. ATPE is a teacher association that "does not endorse candidates", its site says. In its 2026 candidate survey on Teach the Vote, he wrote: "Our state's basic allotment should be doubled, affixed to inflation, and based on student enrollment rather than attendance." The basic allotment is the state's base funding per student. His platform says, "I support pay increases for school workers".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing and accountability. He opposes using the state test to rate schools and wants the elected board consulted on accountability changes. His platform says, of STAAR, the state's standardized tests: "I am against using the STAAR to grade public schools’ accountability scores". On House Bill 8 of 2025, the testing law, he wrote on Teach the Vote: "I do not believe the Commissioner should have the authority to remove or change accountability indicators without consulting the elected SBOE".

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

On Teach the Vote, he answered: "Yes, the SBOE should retain its authority to veto or approve new charter applications on a simple majority vote".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum, library books and religion. His platform opposes the Bluebonnet Learning curriculum, while his survey answer criticizes it without pledging to remove it. His platform says: "I am against the state-developed Bluebonnet Learning curriculum." Bluebonnet Learning is the reading and math materials written by the Texas Education Agency under House Bill 1605 of 2023.

His answer on Teach the Vote is narrower: "I would ensure the Bluebonnet Learning instructional materials are error-free, pedagogically-sound, developmentally-appropriate, and student-centered ... Unfortunately, Bluebonnet Learning is currently none of these things." In the same answer, he opposes the extra state money for districts that adopt the materials, writing, "I believe in local control". He does not pledge to remove them from the approved list.

  • On the 2025-26 social studies rewrite, his answer on Teach the Vote asks for "Much more weight than the SBOE is currently giving educators" and for content advisors with classroom experience.
  • His platform says: "I believe local communities should have the freedom to decide what books belong in their own school libraries".

Social media

  • Curriculum. On June 4, 2026, he posted: "When we flip this seat in November, I will listen to educators, not extremists, on how to prepare our students for the future".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

He wants the board to have more power over certification rules than the law now gives it. Asked about the board's power over those rules, he wrote on Teach the Vote: "Yes. The SBOE is a duly-elected body, and it serves as an important check on the rulemaking actions. The SBOE should also have the ability to amend specific provisions of rules back to the SBEC rather than simply approve or veto rules".

The SBEC is the State Board for Educator Certification, the separate board that proposes those rules. Section 21.042 bars the State Board of Education from changing them, so his proposal would take a change in the law.

His platform also targets the Reading Academies, the reading training for teachers that came out of House Bill 3, the 2019 school finance law: "That's why I’ll fight to reform the Reading Academies so they actually help educators improve reading outcomes." The platform says he would phase out "online-only modules in favor of skilled trainers" and seek "funding for math and literacy coaches, math and literacy training for teachers".

Campaign pledge

His platform says: "College for all? No. College access for all? Yes."

Coretta Mallet-Fontenot, State Board of Education, District 4

Won the unexpired term that runs to 2028. The Associated Press called the race over Republican Tammie Nielsen, whom Gov. Greg Abbott appointed to the seat in August, as the Texas Tribune's results page and voter guide show. The result is not certified.

In brief

Mallet-Fontenot has written against a voucher bill and for limiting new charter applications, and co-signed an op-ed against a state takeover of Houston schools.

The seat is on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards.

In 2025 she urged a House committee to vote no on a voucher bill. In 2022 she wrote that she would limit new charter applications. In 2019 she co-signed an op-ed against a state takeover of Houston schools.

She has never held an office with recorded votes on education policy. In 2021, on a Houston district advisory committee, she voted against a plan with exemptions for hiring noncertified vocational teachers. We found no statement on alternative certification or teacher residencies.

Background and powers of the office

Her campaign describes her as a "27 year Houston ISD educator" on its site, meaning the Houston Independent School District. The site lists elementary, middle-school and high-school teaching, literacy coaching and testing coordination.

She now works for the Houston Federation of Teachers, the Houston teachers' union, as "Organizer / Teacher Leader Program Director", the union's staff page shows.

She lost the 2022 District 4 Democratic runoff to Staci Childs, 41.9% to 58.1%, as the results on Teach the Vote show. Teach the Vote is the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators. A Texas AFT post says the district's precinct chairs, who are local party officials, chose her for the 2026 ballot on August 15, 2026. Texas AFT is the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers.

The seat carries the powers of the State Board of Education set out at the start of this section, under Education Code §7.101.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing and state takeovers. Her campaign criticizes the state test and decisions made by noneducators.
