Voting record

She has never held an office with recorded votes on education policy.

In March 2021 she voted against a District of Innovation plan for the Houston school district, as an employee member of the district's District Advisory Committee, an advisory body. A District of Innovation plan lets a district exempt itself from some state rules. The Houston Chronicle article of April 2, 2021 says this plan included exemptions for "the hiring of noncertified vocational teachers". The committee rejected it 21-10. In the same Chronicle article, she said, "I don’t think the district’s intention necessarily matters when you look at the law".

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations. Texas AFT's committee lists her, but the Texas State Teachers Association does not. Texas AFT's political committee listed her for the November 2026 general election as of October 1, in an archived copy of its list. Her campaign site lists four union presidents as individual endorsers: Jackie Anderson of the Houston Federation of Teachers, Candis Houston of Aldine AFT, Zeph Capo of Texas AFT and Shonda Below of Northeast AFT. She is not on the Texas State Teachers Association's lists, including its general-election list.

Money. The Houston Federation of Teachers gave $1,000 on October 16, 2026, for the general election, as the union's report and her report show.

Advocacy groups. Community Voices for Public Education, a Houston public-school group, endorsed her. It said it "will be supporting our endorsed candidates through block-walks, phone banking, donations", which is a stated plan, not a record of work done. The Texas Freedom Network endorsed every Democrat on the board ballot.

Charter or choice groups. We found none for her. A report shows that Charter Schools Now PAC gave her opponent, Nielsen, $1,000 on September 14, 2026.

What was not found

We found no statements by her on the board's review of certification rules, alternative certification, teacher residencies, Bluebonnet Learning by name, library books or the Permanent School Fund. We found no survey answer from her to the Association of Texas Professional Educators. We could not confirm the reported year, 2013, or the result of her race for the Houston school board.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. In a Democratic-club questionnaire answer posted on her FAQ page, which is undated, she wrote that public funds, "including vouchers", "must strengthen classrooms, not corporate profits". The answer does not call for repealing the state's voucher program.

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

She wrote in the League of Women Voters Houston guide for the May 2026 runoff, on page 3: "While SBOE doesn’t set pay, it should publicly advocate for competitive wages".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing and accountability. In her survey answer on Teach the Vote, she wrote that the board's role "should be one of strong oversight, transparency, and advocacy ... Testing should support meaningful learning - not excessive testing or punitive outcomes".

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

She opposes unlimited charter growth but calls charter schools part of public education. Her campaign home page says Texas "has allowed unchecked charter growth without proper oversight ... I oppose the unlimited expansion of charter schools that diverts resources from our neighborhood public schools".

In the survey of the Association of Texas Professional Educators on Teach the Vote, she wrote that the board should keep its veto "and the Board should also have a role in reviewing significant charter expansion requests". She also wrote there that "Charter schools are part of Texas’s public education system".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum, library books and religion. Her answers favor optional state materials, criticize book bans and limit religion in the curriculum to teaching about it.

  • She wrote on Teach the Vote that state review materials "should serve as optional tools, not prescriptions". She does not name Bluebonnet Learning.
  • Her FAQ page calls "book bans, curriculum fights, and one-size-fits-all rules" state overreach.
  • She wrote in the League of Women Voters Houston guide, on page 3: "Curriculum may teach about religion’s role in history and culture but should not promote or favor any belief system".

Statement or interview

  • Curriculum and charters. After the board's April 2026 social studies and reading-list votes, she told the Austin Chronicle, in a story of May 7, 2026: "They’re moving away from historically accurate curriculum, fact-based instruction". The Chronicle wrote that, asked for the most pressing problem, "Bush argued it’s charter schools".

Statement or interview

  • Curriculum. In a KUT story of October 15, 2026, she said: "I'm seeing that the state board and what they're passing is telling our students what to think and not teaching them how to think".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

She wants the board to keep its veto over certification rules and to set rigorous preparation standards. She wrote in the League of Women Voters Houston guide, on page 3: "The SBOE can strengthen teacher support by setting rigorous, practical preparation standards, protecting certification pathways, and ensuring ongoing professional development aligned to classroom needs".

On the board's review of certification rules, she wrote on Teach the Vote: "Yes, the State Board of Education should retain its authority to review and, when necessary, veto SBEC rulemaking. This oversight helps ensure certification policies are fair, transparent, and supportive of educator professionalism and retention". The SBEC is the State Board for Educator Certification, the separate board that proposes those rules.

Her home page, as quoted in the Tribune guide, says she "will fight for policies that reduce paperwork, provide resources, improve retention, and restore dignity to the teaching profession".

Other

Campaign pledge

She is the only one of the five new candidates in this section whom we found addressing the Permanent School Fund, the state's endowment for public schools. On her FAQ page she wrote: "I understand the questions to ask and how to ensure investments are sound, transparent, and equitable".

Voting record

Bush has never held an office with recorded votes.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations. Texas AFT and the Texas State Teachers Association both endorsed her for the general election, and Education Austin endorsed her. Texas AFT, the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, endorsed her through its political committee on its May 26 runoff list, shown in an archived copy. It endorsed her again for the general election on July 24, 2026.

The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed her for the general election, as its general-election list shows. In March it had endorsed her primary opponent, Kevin Jackson, on its primary list. Education Austin, a union of Austin school employees, endorsed her, according to the Tribune guide.

Labor endorsement. The Texas AFL-CIO, the state labor federation, joined Texas AFT's July 24, 2026 general-election endorsement. That is a labor endorsement, not an education one.

Money. Teacher groups gave to her runoff and general-election campaigns, and on each item the payer's report and hers differ in amount, date or form.

  • The Texas State Teachers Association PAC gave on April 9, 2026, which by date falls in the runoff. The PAC's report shows $2,000, and her report lists $2,500 the same day. The two differ.
  • The Association of Texas Professional Educators PAC gave $2,500 for the May 2026 runoff. The PAC's report dates it May 12, and her report dates it May 16. This was a contribution, not an endorsement.
  • The Texas State Teachers Association PAC gave $1,000 for the general election. The PAC's report dates it August 13, and her report dates it August 20.
  • Texas AFT COPE gave $1,200 for the general election. The payer's report lists "Public event sponsorship" on September 12, an in-kind item, meaning goods or services rather than money. Her report lists a $1,200 contribution on September 14.

Advocacy groups. The Texas Freedom Network endorsed every Democrat on the board ballot, in its slate.

Charter or choice groups. We found none for Bush. Charter Schools Now PAC endorsed and funded her runoff opponent, Stephanie Limon Bazan, as Teach the Vote and the PAC's report show.

What was not found

We found no statements by Bush naming Bluebonnet Learning, the Houston takeover, uncertified teachers, alternative certification by name or teacher residencies. We found no testimony by her and no Raise Your Hand Texas forum with her. We could not confirm her reported answers to a Ballotpedia survey.

Michelle Palmer, State Board of Education, District 6

Won a seat held by Republicans. The Associated Press called the race over Republican Tiffany Nelson, and Palmer led by about 1.4 percentage points in unofficial returns, as the Texas Tribune's results page shows. The result is not certified.

In brief

Palmer, a history and government teacher, vowed in 2022 to vote against all new charter applications and in 2026 called for pausing approvals.

The seat is on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards.

In 2026 she wrote that she would pause new charter approvals until current charters are audited. In a 2020 questionnaire, she answered "Strongly Disagree" to a statement supporting school choice, including vouchers. We found no statement naming the 2025 voucher law.

On certification rules, she wrote that she favors the elected board over the appointed certification board. We found no statement on alternative certification or teacher residencies.

Background and powers of the office

Palmer is a history and government teacher who has taught since 2009, as the Texas Tribune voter guide shows.

She was the Democratic nominee for this seat in 2020 and 2022 and lost both times, as her page on Teach the Vote shows. That site is run by the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association.

She is a member of Aldine AFT, a local teachers' union, as a Texas AFT post shows. Texas AFT is the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers. She has held no public office.

The seat carries the powers of the State Board of Education, or SBOE, set out at the start of this section, under Education Code §7.101.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We checked her Bluesky account, rabidreader1970.bsky.social, which had 978 feed items, seven of them her own posts. We could not read her Facebook account, palmerfortexased.

On November 11, 2025, she posted on Bluesky: "I signed this petition organized by Texas Freedom Network". The petition was about the board's social studies overhaul.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. In a 2020 questionnaire for iVoterGuide, she answered "Strongly Disagree" to "I support school choice, including voucher programs, tax credits, charter schools, private schools, and home schools". iVoterGuide is a voter guide run by AFA Action that says it informs faith-based voters.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing. She has written against required testing and against moving power from the elected board to the state agency. In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote: "I suggest we get rid of testing (at least not require it for graduation) and instead use a portfolio system." In 2026 she wrote there: "Elected board members have been slowly having their power stripped and given to the appointed TEA. I am against this completely". The TEA is the Texas Education Agency, the state agency that runs public education.

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

She wrote against new charters in both her 2022 and 2026 surveys. In her 2022 survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "I have vowed to vote against all new charter school applications." In 2026 she wrote there: "I would put a pause on new charter approvals until the current charter systems can be audited".

Statement or interview

  • Charters and reading lists. In a Houston Chronicle editorial board piece of October 10, 2026, she said: "Should kids in Amarillo be reading the same thing my students in Aldine are reading? ... I don't think they should." The editorial board wrote that she is open to charters "dedicated to certain populations, such as kids with special education needs" and would otherwise seek "a moratorium on new charter school systems".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum. Her survey answer calls for teaching climate change. Her platform page supports teaching consent and opposes mentioning Moses in U.S. history. In her 2026 survey on Teach the Vote, she wrote: "Science standards need to include climate change for instance".

Her undated platform page, which still describes the 2022 race, says "Moses should not be mentioned in the US History curriculum". The page also supports "actively teaching consent".

On state-written materials, she wrote on Teach the Vote: "I use OER materials as my textbook in all of my courses and none of them are TEA developed". OER means open educational resources, which are openly licensed teaching materials.

Statement or interview

  • Sex education. In OutSmart in October 2020, she said: "Abstinence-only sex education is failing the students of Texas".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

She favors the elected board over the appointed certification board and has linked certification to her charter position. On the certification board's rules, she wrote in 2026 on Teach the Vote: "SBOE is elected whereas SBEC is appointed. I will always choose the more accountable and pro-democracy way to do things". The SBEC is the State Board for Educator Certification, which proposes those rules.

In 2022 she wrote on Teach the Vote that educators and groups such as the association "should be met with regarding who to appoint to curriculum committees, revising of teacher certification requirements, and revising of graduation requirements". In the same survey, she gave as a reason for opposing charters that they "do not require teacher certification and do not give yearly contracts".

In 2026 she said the board "should help to improve certification pathways to increase the number of trained and certified teachers in TX", in the League of Women Voters Houston guide.

Statement or interview

  • Teachers. In a Texas Tribune story of October 22, 2026, she said: "Teachers see what's happening, and they're kind of sick of it".

Voting record

Palmer has never held an office with recorded votes.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations. Texas AFT endorsed her on July 24, 2026. The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed her for the general election, as its endorsement list shows.

Labor endorsement. The Texas AFL-CIO, the state labor federation, endorsed her in the same announcement. That is a labor endorsement, not an education one.

Money, November 2026 general election. Texas AFT COPE and the Texas State Teachers Association PAC gave to her general-election campaign.

  • Texas AFT COPE gave $5,000. The payer's report dates it October 5, and her report dates it October 2. The dates differ.
  • The Texas State Teachers Association PAC gave $250. The payer's report dates it August 13, and her report dates it October 2.
  • In an earlier cycle, iVoterGuide lists money she received in 2020 from the Association of Texas Professional Educators.

Advocacy groups. Community Voices for Public Education endorsed her, and so did the Texas Freedom Network, in its slate.

Charter or choice groups. We found none for Palmer. Her opponent, Nelson, received a $2,500 contribution and $32,483 in in-kind digital ads from Charter Schools Now PAC, as one report and another show. In-kind help is given as goods or services rather than money. Nelson also received in-kind texting from Texans for Educational Freedom, and the Tribune guide gives a figure of $90,387, including the texting.

What was not found

We found no statements by Palmer naming Bluebonnet Learning or the 2025 voucher law. We found none on the Permanent School Fund, alternative certification, teacher residencies or the Houston takeover, and none on uncertified teachers apart from her 2022 remark about charters. We did not transcribe two audio interviews on Off the Kuff, a Houston politics blog, from 2022 and September 16, 2026. We could not confirm her reported 2020 and 2022 vote shares.

Tiffany Clark, State Board of Education, District 13 (re-elected)

Re-elected. The Associated Press called the race over Republican Carlos "Charlie" Garza, as the Texas Tribune's results page shows. The result is not certified. A post by the Association of Texas Professional Educators after the March primary named a different Republican opponent, April Moore, on Teach the Vote. We did not resolve the difference.

In brief

On recorded votes, Clark opposed the social studies standards, the 2026 reading list and every charter applicant but one.

She sits on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards. She is also on its Committee on School Initiatives, which reviews every certification-board rule and the charter applications, as the January 2025 minutes show.

She voted no on the 2026 required reading list, which includes Bible passages, and on every recorded social studies vote. On charters, she voted against allowing every applicant on a named roll call in 2025 and 2026 except Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy.

On certification rules, she made the committee motions that let two rule packages take effect in January and September 2025. Her votes on later packages, including the 2026 rules written to carry out House Bill 2 of 2025, are not recorded by name.

We found no statement from her on those House Bill 2 certification rules or on teacher residencies.

Background and powers of the office

Clark was a middle- and high-school counselor for 10 years, as the DeSoto Independent School District records. The district says she served on its school board from 2017 to May 2023, as vice president in 2021-2022.

She took her seat on the State Board of Education on January 1, 2025, for an unexpired term, as her board biography shows. The biography says she is an adjunct professor at the University of North Texas at Dallas, "where she teaches future educators".

She sits on the Committee on School Initiatives, as the January 2025 minutes show. That committee reviews the charter applications and every rule proposed by the State Board for Educator Certification, the separate board that writes certification rules.

The office's powers are set out at the start of this section, under Education Code §7.101.

Record by issue

General notes

Campaign pledge

Her undated campaign home page pledges to "Advocate for a balanced curriculum that includes an improved testing instrument aligned with Texas standards," to "Fight for the mental health of students, staff, and teachers," and "STOP BOOK BANS!"

She did not answer the 2026 survey of the Association of Texas Professional Educators, as her page on Teach the Vote, its candidate-information site, shows. The 2024 League of Women Voters guide lists her as unopposed with no answers. We found no pledge on vouchers, charters or teacher preparation.

Social media

We did not retrieve the accounts listed on her site, on Facebook, Instagram, Threads and TikTok, or her campaign newsletters. We read no posts.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Statement or interview

Testing and teacher preparation. Her 2024 comment to the Legislature questioned tests as a measure of students and teachers. In written comment for the House Public Education Committee's August 13, 2024 hearing on teacher certification, she wrote that teachers take on debt for more education without more pay. She also wrote there that "it takes more than a test to define a student or teacher. When we talk about teacher certification it has to go back to standards at the home..." In the same comment, she wrote that STAAR, the state's standardized test, "isn't relatable to all students".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Statement or interview

Curriculum and religion. She has criticized the social studies draft and the Bible passages on the reading list.

  • During board debate on the social studies draft on April 10, 2026, she said: "It seems as if, when it comes to Black and brown information being in these TEKS, we continue to undermine our experiences". The TEKS are the state's curriculum standards.
  • In a CNN report of June 2026 on the reading list with Bible passages, she said she and some Christian constituents believe "Bible lessons should be taught on Sundays". She also said: "Teachers know what their students need... Our students need to focus on reading comprehension".
  • In November 2024, before she was seated, the Texas Freedom Network reported that "Clark said she would've voted against the curriculum," meaning Bluebonnet Learning, the reading and math materials written by the Texas Education Agency.

Voting record

On charters, she voted against allowing every applicant on a named roll call in 2025 and 2026 except one. The exception was Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy, which she voted to allow in committee on June 25, 2025. On June 27, 2025, she then voted not to veto it. She voted for vetoing Valenta Academy and was absent for the committee vote on the 2026 charter list.

She voted no on every recorded vote on the social studies standards and on the 2026 reading list. Two of the social studies votes are as reported by the Tribune.

On the American Indian/Native Studies course, she voted yes in committee, no on postponing it and yes on suspending the rules to take it up.

On certification rules, as the committee member who made the motions, she let two packages take effect. Certification-rule decisions before 2025 predate her service. Where the minutes do not show her individual vote, the table says "not recorded".

33 rows

As a DeSoto school board member. On August 30, 2020, as the district faced possible state oversight, she voted against accepting the superintendent's resignation agreement and against naming an acting superintendent, as a Dallas Morning News story shows. Both motions carried 4-3. The district credits her with adding "African-American and Mexican American studies courses to the district curriculum".

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations. Texas AFT, the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, endorsed her through its political committee for the March 2026 primary round and the general election. Archived copies of its May 26 list and October 1 list show both. The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed her for the general election, as its endorsement list shows.

Money. Her own report lists one teacher-group contribution. The Texas State Teachers Association PAC reports two more that do not appear in her reports.

  • The Texas American Federation of Teachers gave $250 on September 18, 2024, for the November 2024 general election, as her report shows.
  • The Texas State Teachers Association PAC reports $1,000 to her on February 19, 2026, for the March primary, in one report. It reports $500 on August 13, 2026, for the general election, in another. Neither appears in her own reports through October 24, 2026, and we did not establish why.

Advocacy groups. The Texas Freedom Network endorsed every Democrat on the board ballot, in its announcement. Charter or choice groups: we found none. Her campaign endorsements page is empty. We found no education group backing her opponent.

What was not found

We found no statement by Clark on the 2025 House Bill 2 certification rules or on teacher residencies, none on vouchers or charters, and no 2024 platform. A search for her named votes on DeSoto items directed by the state conservator, the official the state appointed to oversee the district, also found nothing. We did not retrieve her campaign newsletters or two 2026 television segments. We could not confirm quotations said to come from WFAA, a Dallas television station, and from the Houston Chronicle.

Dana Van de Walker, candidate, State Board of Education, District 8

Race not called. She led the Republican incumbent, Audrey G. Young, by 569 votes in Associated Press data on November 9, 2026. The incumbent has not conceded, as the Texas Tribune shows. The Houston Chronicle reported on November 5 that the margin is within the range for a recount if Young requests one.

In brief

Van de Walker, whose race is not called, wrote that alternative certification should be the exception and that charter schools also need certified teachers.

The District 8 seat is on the elected State Board of Education, which sets curriculum standards.

She wrote that she would fight to remove the Ten Commandments and religiously influenced curriculum from public schools. She also supports an across-the-board raise for teachers and an end to state school takeovers.

She has never held an office with recorded votes. Her certification views come from survey answers on Teach the Vote and in a League of Women Voters guide. We found no statement from her on teacher residencies.

Background and powers of the office

Van de Walker is "Honors and International Director" at Lone Star College, as the college directory shows. The Houston Chronicle says she teaches government there, and on February 15, 2026 it called her "a first-time candidate".

Her campaign site says she taught English as a second language in Korea and "earned her CELTA teaching certificate". The site also says she holds an Ed.D. in higher education leadership from 2021.

She graded STAAR exams, the state's standardized tests, for ETS, a testing organization, from 2015 to 2018, as her page on Teach the Vote shows. Teach the Vote is the candidate-information site of the Association of Texas Professional Educators. These sources state no Texas K-12 classroom job and no Texas teaching certificate.

The District 8 seat carries the powers of the State Board of Education, or SBOE, set out at the start of this section, under Education Code §7.101.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We checked her Facebook campaign page, Instagram and TikTok, all named dana4txsboe8. We could not read any of them directly, so we read no posts.

School funding and teacher pay

Campaign pledge

School funding and teacher pay; state takeovers. She wrote in the League of Women Voters Houston guide: "I support an across-the-board increase in teacher salaries and an end to state school takeovers".

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Campaign pledge

Testing. She wrote on Teach the Vote: "This experience taught me that we need greater oversight in our standardized testing AND that we need to develop more holistic approaches to student evaulation".

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

In her survey answer on Teach the Vote, she wrote that she would keep the board's veto and limit charter expansion "as they have historically been held to lower accountability standards". The same answer keeps charters as "an option for providing a highly-specialized curriculum, such as foreign language immersion".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum, library books and religion. She pledged to fight to remove the Ten Commandments and religiously influenced curriculum and wrote that she opposes book bans. She wrote on Teach the Vote: "I believe that religion has no place in our public schools and will fight to remove the Ten Commandments and any religiously-influenced curriculum ... I am also fiercely opposed to book bans".

In her survey answers on Teach the Vote and in the League of Women Voters Houston guide, she wrote that she favors state approval of common materials "by subject-matter experts" and would have "only 1-2 books" state-mandated per grade.

Statement or interview

  • Curriculum. In a Houston Chronicle story of November 5, 2026, the reporter summarized members' plans to amend the 2026 social studies standards, revisit the reading list and reevaluate Bluebonnet Learning. Bluebonnet Learning is the state-written reading and math materials. She is then quoted: "We’ve been running with that as a day one promise ... We’re really committed to keeping the church out of our state and also uphold academic integrity". In February the Chronicle's editorial board wrote that she is "far more worried about the subpar quality of the Bluebonnet curriculum", in an editorial. In the Chronicle on October 10, 2026, her opponent, Young, answered her criticism of the standards: "It’s always great to handpick one or two standards that you don’t like and inflame the information".

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

She wrote that alternative certification should be the exception and that all schools the board oversees need certified teachers. Her answer on Teach the Vote reads: "It is squarely the responsibility of the SBOE to ensure that our teachers are prepared to be in the classrooms ... Alternative certification programs, while useful, should be the exception, not the rule, in teacher certification. Similarly, I believe that all schools under the purview of the SBOE, including charter schools, need to have certified teachers in the classroom".

In the 2026 general-election League of Women Voters Houston guide, she wrote: "Texas has a teacher crisis. We have too few teachers overall, along with an unacceptable percentage of teachers coming into our districts without certification (or with alternate certification still in progress)".

Statement or interview

  • Teachers. In Livingston on July 9, 2026, she said in a Polk County Enterprise story: "A huge priority of mine is to recruit teachers, pay teachers and keep them here in Texas".

Higher education

Campaign pledge

Her home page lists "AFFORDABLE HIGHER EDUCATION FOR ALL" with "SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE" and "INVESTMENT IN TEXAS PUBLIC SCHOOLS".

Voting record

Van de Walker has never held an office with recorded votes.

Education-oriented backers

Teacher organizations endorsed her, and a charter-school political committee gave to her opponent. Texas AFT, the state affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, endorsed her on July 24, 2026. In the same announcement, the Texas AFL-CIO, the state labor federation, gave her a labor endorsement, not an education one.

The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed her, as its endorsement list shows. Its PAC gave $250 on August 13, 2026, for the general election, as the PAC's report and her report show.

The Texas Freedom Network endorsed the full board slate. Her own endorsements page lists no education organization, and we found no charter or choice backing for her.

Young received $5,000 from Charter Schools Now PAC on April 28, 2025, plus later contributions and in-kind help, as a report shows. In-kind help is given as goods or services rather than money. Young also received in-kind texting from Texans for Educational Freedom, as another report shows.

What was not found

We found no statement by her on the Permanent School Fund, on vouchers in her own words, on teacher residencies or on the Houston takeover by name. We could not confirm two reported items. One is a 2026 primary-guide answer calling for "routes to alternate certification that actually work" and an end to vouchers, in a guide we could not open. The other is criticism of her by Texas Scorecard and the Montgomery County Eagle Forum.

Marisa B. Pérez-Díaz, State Board of Education, District 3

Not on the 2026 ballot. Her term runs to January 1, 2029, her board biography says.

In brief

In 2018 Pérez-Díaz wanted charter expansion halted pending an assessment, and from 2019 to 2025 she voted to allow some new charters and veto others.

State law sets the powers of the State Board of Education. Pérez-Díaz has sat on the board since 2013, and her board biography calls her "the most senior Democrat on the board".

In a 2018 survey, she wrote that she wanted "a halt to the expansion of additional charter schools, until a proper assessment can be made". From 2019 to 2025 she voted to allow some charter applicants and to veto others, and we found no explanation in her own words. In 2022 she voted for a board legislative priority that opposed diverting public dollars from public schools to vouchers.

In the same survey, she wrote that the board's "authority to review and veto rule actions should remain intact" for educator-certification rules. In 2014 she voted to reject a rule on candidates for teacher-preparation programs. We found no statement by her on House Bill 2 of 2025 or on teacher residencies.

Background and powers of the office

Pérez-Díaz was elected in November 2012, took office in 2013 and was re-elected in 2014, 2018, 2022 and 2024. Her board biography calls her "the most senior Democrat on the board".

She worked at the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services and spent "nearly a decade as a district-level administrator in several Texas school districts," the biography says. She is now a vice president at Firstmark Credit Union, and she served as Marisa B. Perez until early 2017, the same biography says.

From 2017 to 2020, she was vice chair of the Committee on School Initiatives, which reviews certification rules. Since 2021 she has served on the School Finance/Permanent School Fund committee, and she was a founding director of the Texas Permanent School Fund Corporation, her board biography says. The Permanent School Fund is the state endowment that helps pay for public schools.

Committee minutes list her as vice chair of the School Finance/Permanent School Fund committee in 2025. The office's powers, under §7.101 of the Education Code, are set out at the start of this section.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

We could not establish any social-media accounts for her and read no posts. ATPE's profile lists only marisabperez.com, which is now a parked page.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. An archived copy of her 2015 campaign page, written in the third person, says that as a new member she "passionately debated and supported the State Board of Education's Anti-Voucher Resolution". We did not check the resolution's date.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers

Statement or interview

Testing and state takeovers. Her remarks came in November 2019, after the state takeover of the Houston Independent School District was announced. She "questioned Morath regarding the process for transitioning from an agency-run board of managers back to a locally elected body," according to ATPE's account. Mike Morath is the commissioner of education.

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

In her 2018 survey for the Association of Texas Professional Educators, or ATPE, a teacher association, she wrote on Teach the Vote: "Overall, the performance of charter schools is unimpressive... It would be my desire to see a halt to the expansion of additional charter schools, until a proper assessment can be made..." Teach the Vote is ATPE's candidate-information site.

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum. The same survey calls the standards "mile wide and inch deep" and says educators "must have a seat at the table".

Statement or interview

Curriculum and religion. Her statements on curriculum concern the 2022 social studies delay, the Bluebonnet Learning materials and the 2026 high school standards.

  • The board delayed the social studies rewrite in 2022. In a signed op-ed in the San Antonio Express-News on September 15, 2022, she wrote: "On Sept. 2, the State Board of Education, or SBOE, failed our educators and students" and "We, the SBOE, are the gatekeepers. We should never be the groundskeepers".
  • Bluebonnet Learning is a set of state-written instructional materials. In FOX 7 Austin's coverage of the board's debate on it in November 2024, she said: "Had it not been for the Christian bias in this content, I do really find value in how a lot of these lessons are laid out." ATPE reported that she raised a "conflict of interest" in the agency being both a vendor and a reviewer of materials.
  • In August 2026, on high school social studies, she said in the Texas Tribune: "Slavery is foundational to this country."

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

In the same survey, she backed keeping the State Board of Education's power over educator-certification rules. Asked whether the board should keep that power, she answered: "Absolutely! SBEC is an appointed board and therefore is answerable to the Commissioner of Education. As an elected body, the SBOE has a responsibility and is accountable to our constituents... the authority to review and veto rule actions should remain intact". In that answer, SBEC is the State Board for Educator Certification and SBOE is the State Board of Education.

She did not answer ATPE's 2022 or 2024 surveys, Teach the Vote shows.

Statement or interview

Her recorded remarks on certification concern the 2022 edTPA decision and uncertified teachers.

  • The board rejected edTPA, a performance assessment the certification board had adopted in place of the existing certification exam. She then represented the board at a July 21, 2022 work session with the certification board. ATPE reported that she "noted that Option C was most aligned with the direction the SBOE wanted to take." In that account, Option C was a performance assessment run as a preparation-program requirement rather than a certification exam.
  • In January 2025, ATPE wrote: "Responding to a question from Perez-Diaz, Morath clarified there is no requirement that newly hired uncertified teachers ever get certified."

Voting record

Charter votes and her 2018 statement, side by side. In 2018 she wrote on Teach the Vote that she wanted "a halt to the expansion of additional charter schools, until a proper assessment can be made". She voted to allow Gathering Place in 2019, Essence Prep and Rocketship in 2021, and Celebrate Dyslexia and Up Excellence in 2023.

In 2025 she voted to allow Mater Academy San Antonio, Fort Worth STEAM Academy and Frank Liu Jr. Academy. She also voted to veto others, as the table shows. We found no explanation in her own words.

Three other named votes of hers differ from those of other Democrats on the board. She voted to keep Bluebonnet Math on the approved list, which passed 13-2 with Democrat Ortega voting no, the minutes show.

In 2023 she voted to change the abortion language in the materials review rubric from "describe" to "promote or encourage," while Democrats Bell-Metereau, Childs and Ortega abstained, the minutes show. In 2014 she voted to reject a certification rule that Democrats Cortez and Dominguez voted to keep, the minutes record.

For Royal Public Schools in 2020, the minutes list her among the no votes on allowing the charter. A table by the Texas Association of School Administrators, a school administrators' group, reportedly lists her position as "Allow". We did not read that table.

Education-oriented backers

The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed her for the November 2024 general election, its 2024 list shows. Its PAC sent her $500 on November 18, 2024, its report shows. The check was never cashed and was voided on April 16, 2025.

Families for Education and Opportunity, a San Antonio political committee whose main purpose we could not establish, gave her $1,000 on October 20, 2025, off-cycle, her report shows. Its other 2025 gifts went mostly to San Antonio city candidates and to Republican board member Audrey Young, its report shows.

For 2018, ATPE's profile says she was "recommended favorably by Texans for Public Education," a group of educators, and endorsed in the primary by the San Antonio Express-News. We found no backing from advocacy or charter groups for the 2024 cycle or later.

What was not found

We searched without result for her 2012 platform and for statements on House Bill 2 of 2025, the school-finance and teacher-pay law, or on teacher residencies. We also found no recorded vote of hers on the 2024 residency rules. We found no social-media posts and no criticism of her by a named organization.

Two items are reported but not confirmed: a 2024 Texas AFT endorsement, known only from an aggregator, and votes on the Permanent School Fund Corporation's board in 2023.

Gustavo Reveles, State Board of Education, District 1

Not on the 2026 ballot. His term runs to January 1, 2029, his board biography says.

In brief

Reveles voted against allowing every charter applicant on a named roll call in 2025 and 2026 except one, and urged a charter moratorium in 2024.

State law sets the powers of the State Board of Education. Reveles won his seat in November 2024 with 50.92% of the vote.

In a 2024 questionnaire, he wrote, "I strongly oppose the use of vouchers, which would further diminish funding for public schools," and called for a moratorium on charter expansion. On the board, the only charter applicant he voted to allow on a named roll call was Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy. He voted no at every recorded vote on the social studies standards. For two of those votes, his position comes from Texas Tribune coverage.

In 2024 he wrote in a League of Women Voters guide that "Districts should have the option to rely on non-certified educators for hard-to-fill subjects," with proper certification to follow. His individual votes on certification rules are not recorded. We found no statement by him on the 2025 certification rules from House Bill 2 or on teacher residencies.

Background and powers of the office

Reveles spent 15 years as a journalist at the El Paso Times and the Fort Worth Star-Telegram and then moved to school-district communications, Canutillo ISD and his board biography say. He worked for the Canutillo school district in 2010-2014 and the El Paso school district in 2014-2022, as Canutillo ISD and his biography show. He went back to Canutillo in June 2022 and is now its executive director of communications.

The San Antonio Report, a San Antonio news site, shows him winning the seat in November 2024 with 50.92% of the vote. He took office on January 1, 2025. He sits on the Committee on Instruction, which handles the curriculum standards, the January 2025 minutes show.

The office's powers, under §7.101 of the Education Code, are set out at the start of this section.

Record by issue

General notes

Social media

The only campaign site listed in 2024 is a Facebook group link, which we did not retrieve. We could not establish an X, Instagram or Bluesky account for him and read no posts.

Vouchers and education savings accounts

Campaign pledge

Vouchers. In his 2024 San Antonio Report questionnaire, he wrote: "I strongly oppose the use of vouchers, which would further diminish funding for public schools."

Charter schools

Campaign pledge

In the same questionnaire, he wrote that the state should "place a moratorium on the expansion of charter programs until the public receives a true assessment of how charter schools are performing".

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools

Campaign pledge

Curriculum and religion. His 2024 answer in the League of Women Voters guide says "A clear separation of church and state should be a guiding principle".

Statement or interview

Curriculum and the role of teachers. His statements concern keeping politics out of the curriculum and the place of teachers in writing the standards. After his 2024 win, he said in the San Antonio Report: "We need to make sure to develop a curriculum that focuses on academics, focuses on pedagogy, and really steps away from politics and personal beliefs."

The Texan reported that in a September 2026 interview he called teacher input on the standards an "afterthought" or a "box to check" and described the process as "altered and diminished". In the same Texan account, he said: "I'm not an educator, and I would never call myself an educator."

Teacher preparation and certification

Campaign pledge

In 2024 he said uncertified teachers should be allowed in some cases and that voucher funds should not go to programs led by uncertified teachers. The League of Women Voters asked whether uncertified teachers should be allowed in Texas classrooms. He answered: "In some cases, yes. Districts should have the option to rely on non-certified educators for hard-to-fill subjects."

His condition was that "an emergency certification should be followed by proper certification within a certain amount of time". His opponent answered "No" in the same guide.

In the same cycle he wrote in the San Antonio Report: "We also must make sure that voucher funds are not spent on programs led by uncertified teachers."

Voting record

He voted against allowing every charter applicant on a named roll call in 2025 and 2026 except Unidos Soccer Leadership Academy. He voted to allow Unidos in committee on June 25, 2025, and then voted not to veto it on June 27, 2025. He also voted to veto Valenta Academy.

He voted no on every recorded vote on the social studies standards, two of them as reported by the Tribune, and on the 2026 reading list. On the American Indian/Native Studies course, he voted yes in committee, no on postponing it and yes on suspending the rules to take it up. His individual votes on certification rules are not recorded.

Certification-rule decisions before 2025 predate his service.

Education-oriented backers

The Texas State Teachers Association endorsed him for the November 2024 general election, its 2024 list shows. Its PAC sent him $1,000 on August 19, 2024, its report shows. The check was never cashed and was voided on April 16, 2025.

His own 2024-2026 reports show no education money, and we found no backing from advocacy or charter groups.

What was not found

We searched without result for statements on the 2025 House Bill 2 certification rules or teacher residencies, for statements on charters as a board member, and for social-media posts.

Two items are reported but not confirmed: a 2024 Texas AFT endorsement, known only from aggregators, and a quotation on certification from KVIA, an El Paso television station.

How to read this document

Scope. This document covers the Democratic winners of Texas's statewide races, the State Board of Education and the Texas Supreme Court, as requested. At the requester's direction on November 9, 2026, it adds the U.S. senator-elect and the two sitting State Board Democrats who were not on the ballot. It leaves out the winners for two courts: the Court of Criminal Appeals, which hears criminal cases only, and the Fifteenth Court of Appeals.

Under Senate Bill 1045 of 2023, the Fifteenth Court has "exclusive intermediate appellate jurisdiction" over cases brought by or against state agencies. Those include the Texas Education Agency, the state agency that oversees public schools. The law applies to appeals perfected on or after September 1, 2024. On that date it moved to the new court the cases of that kind pending in other courts of appeals that had been filed on or after September 1, 2023.

Result status. The Associated Press has called every race here except State Board District 8. Nothing is certified, and the state's official count, the canvass, ends December 7, 2026, as the Secretary of State shows. The record runs to November 9, 2026.

Kinds of evidence.

  • A pledge is a promise about future conduct.
  • A statement is something the person said or wrote, dated, with the venue.
  • A social media post is quoted from the platform named.
  • A recorded vote is printed in the House or Senate Journal or in State Board minutes.
  • An authored bill is one the person filed, with its outcome.
  • An official act is a vote or action in a prior office, such as a school board.
  • A court ruling is given with the judge's role, the question and the outcome.
  • A backer is an endorsement, contribution or independent expenditure, with the election stage.

Three rules matter most. A pledge is not policy. A vote on a large bill is a vote on the bill, not on each provision. A court ruling is not a policy view.

Party comparisons. Some vote tables note that most members of the person's party in that chamber, or on the State Board, voted the other way. That note comes from our own count of the journal or minutes roll call. It lets you see where a person's vote differed from most of their party's, and we do not give exact counts.

How sources appear. Links sit in the text. A quotation or record with no qualifier was confirmed on the linked page. Where you see "according to" or "as reported by", the item comes from a news account or other secondary source.

What "nothing found" means. We searched the named sources without result. It does not mean the person has no view.

Limits. We could not read posts on X, Facebook and Instagram for most people here, and each profile lists the accounts we checked. Some news pages, aggregator sites and Ballotpedia questionnaires could not be opened. The State Board minutes record individual votes for only some decisions, and most show only "carried" or a tally.

Looking ahead. The section "Implications for the future" gives our estimates of what will happen next, and the section "How we made the estimates" gives the rules and sources behind them. Everything else in this document is record.

How we made the estimates

This section gives the definitions, dates, rules and sources behind the estimates in "Implications for the future". The winners' own words and votes are in the profiles. These two sections are the only parts of this document that look ahead.

What the five words mean

Our estimates use five words, each tied to a date:

  • very likely: we would be surprised if it did not happen
  • likely: we expect it to happen, with real doubt
  • uncertain: we see no clear lean either way
  • unlikely: we expect it not to happen, with real doubt
  • very unlikely: we would be surprised if it happened

These are our estimates as of November 9, 2026, and no source offers odds.

What the dates mean

"By May 31, 2027" means passed by both chambers before the regular session ends, under the 140-day limit in the constitution. Afterward the governor can call special sessions under article IV, section 8: "The Governor may, on extraordinary occasions, convene the Legislature".

The budget is the one law both chambers must pass every two years, so the two parties must agree on it. Under article IV, section 14 of the constitution, the governor "may object to one or more of such items, and approve the other portion of the bill". That line-item veto removes an item of spending but cannot repeal a program or change an amount.

June 20, 2027 is the veto deadline for bills passed at the session's end. The governor has "twenty days after such adjournment" under article IV, section 14.

The Senate adopts its rules at the start of the session, which opens January 12, 2027. Under the current rules, 16 senators can change them.

20 rows

The firmest estimates concern what one office can do alone or what current law already requires.

The rules and evidence behind each estimate

The Senate's rules and the lieutenant governor. Democrats won every statewide race here, as the Associated Press calls showed on November 9, 2026. That day the MultiState tracker projected that they hold the House and Republicans the Senate.

So the first changes are those an office can make alone: appointments subject to Senate consent, agency decisions, audits, vetoes and choices about what to argue in court. New laws that Senate Republicans oppose are unlikely to pass.

We rate it likely, by January 31, 2027, that Republicans cut the lieutenant governor's power over committees and bills, as the outgoing lieutenant governor, Dan Patrick, urged on November 9. Every estimate that needs the Senate depends on it. If the lieutenant governor keeps her powers after the Senate's rules vote in January 2027, estimates that need the Senate become less firm. The section "Texas Legislature" gives the projected seats in each chamber, the votes each action takes and the comparable cases.

Vouchers and education savings accounts. All six winners who served in the Legislature voted against Senate Bill 2 of 2025, the House and Senate journals record. It created the education savings accounts, which Hinojosa has pledged to end.

Repeal by May 31, 2027 is very unlikely, since the Senate majority that passed the program remains. Republican Senator Paul Bettencourt, who led its passage, now says the Legislature should review the 2026-27 results, the Tribune reported.

In Arizona, Governor Katie Hobbs's first-year attempt to repeal the universal part of her state's program "went nowhere" against Republican lawmakers, The 74 reported. She then worked with them on accountability, the Houston Chronicle reported.

Eckhardt, as comptroller, is very likely to keep the program running through the 2026-27 school year and audit it, by August 31, 2027. Under chapter 29 of the Education Code, the comptroller "shall establish and administer" the program and must have a private firm audit it yearly. The comptroller alone writes its rules, sets application deadlines and suspends providers that break them.

The comptroller reported more than 102,000 students awarded accounts on June 10, 2026. The Tribune put participation at roughly 110,000 in November, a different measure.

Money for the program in fiscal years 2028 and 2029 is uncertain, by June 20, 2027. The Legislature must set each two-year amount under §29.3521, so House budget writers, the governor's line-item veto, as the Texas Tribune describes it, and the Senate all affect it. We do not estimate an amount.

What to watch: six repeal bills filed on November 9, 2026, none yet in committee: House Bills 164, 646, 675 and 735 and Senate Bills 106 and 294.

School funding and teacher pay. Hinojosa, Goodwin and Talarico voted for House Bill 2 of 2025 at second reading, third reading and concurrence, the House Journals of April 16, April 17 and May 29, 2025 record. Rosenthal voted no on the final version.

The House Bill 2 raises are very likely to stay funded by June 20, 2027. The law requires districts to keep paying them, under §48.158.

A new across-the-board raise is uncertain by the same date. The Senate passed House Bill 2 31 to 0, so it is not a known opponent of raises.

The open questions are revenue and what each chamber asks in return. Hinojosa's campaign site pledges higher teacher pay with no dollar figure.

Under article III, section 49a of the constitution, "No bill containing an appropriation shall be considered as passed or be sent to the Governor for consideration until and unless the Comptroller of Public Accounts endorses his certificate thereon showing that the amount appropriated is within the amount estimated to be available". The same section lets four-fifths of each chamber override that limit in an emergency, and the certificate concerns available money, not policy.

The comptroller's revenue estimate in January 2027 moves the voucher-money, new-raise and preparation-funding estimates.

What to watch: the first House budget, and bills on the basic allotment, the state's base funding per student, filed on November 9, 2026.

Testing, accountability and state takeovers. Hinojosa, Goodwin, Talarico, Rosenthal and Johnson voted against House Bill 8 of 2025, which replaced STAAR, as the House Journal and the profiles record. The Senate passed it 21 to 5, so a law that cancels its new tests or pauses the A-F ratings is very unlikely by August 31, 2028.

Pausing the ratings without a new law is also very unlikely by then. House Bill 8 requires ratings to be public "not later than August 15 of each year" and allows "Not Rated" only in listed cases, such as a declared disaster. Hinojosa's pledge to pause the system therefore needs a new law or fits only those cases.

With a commissioner she chose in office, a change to the standards or measures behind the ratings is likely by August 31, 2028, under §39.0541. Authority does not show intent. Standards not adopted by the July 15 before a school year leave that year's ratings "based on the performance standards in effect for the preceding school year", House Bill 8 says.

A commissioner chosen by Hinojosa, confirmed or serving while the Senate considers the nomination, is likely to run the agency by May 31, 2027. Article IV, section 12 of the constitution, which governs the governor's appointments, does not mention an acting appointment: one made during a session "shall be with the advice and consent of two-thirds of the Senate present", under article IV, section 12(b).

Morath's appointment expires January 10, 2027, as reported by Texas Public Radio, KPRC and the Houston Chronicle, though the statute gives no date. Hinojosa can name an acting commissioner immediately, according to the Texas Tribune's reading of the law.

Confirmation of her nominee is uncertain by May 31, 2027. It takes 21 of 31 senators if all attend. Democrats hold 12 seats on projected results, the Texas Tribune reported on November 5, 2026, so at least nine Republicans must vote yes.

A minority has blocked nominees. Senate Democrats blocked Secretary of State David Whitley in 2019, according to The Week. The Senate rejected Don McLeroy as State Board chair in 2009, as reported by the National Center for Science Education.

The Senate's vote on Hinojosa's nominee for commissioner, if it comes between January and May 2027 under §7.051, moves the agency, confirmation, ratings and charter-veto estimates.

Hinojosa pledged to return Houston's school district to its elected board. The commissioner's letter of May 30, 2025 extended the board of managers' authority "until June 1, 2027". The letter says: "On or around June 1, 2027, I will announce the transition timeline for the return of elected trustees to the district's governing board".

We rate it very likely that the state announces a timeline for returning Houston's elected trustees by December 31, 2027. We rate it very unlikely that they hold all the board's seats by then. The commissioner's Houston announcement, promised in the agency's letter, moves both Houston estimates.

What to watch: the nominee's hearing before the Senate Nominations Committee, which hears appointees first, and the field test of the new tests on February 1 to 5, 2027.

Charter schools. The winners split on charter schools. Talarico wrote in 2022 that high-quality nonprofit charters have a role. Goodwin, Rosenthal, Mallet-Fontenot, Palmer, Van de Walker and Reveles have asked for fewer new charters or a pause.

We found no charter pledge in Hinojosa's 2026 campaign.

A binding pause needs a law, so we rate one very unlikely by May 31, 2027. Without one, the commissioner can propose fewer new charters. The commissioner alone approves expansions of existing ones: under §12.114, "A revision of a charter of an open-enrollment charter school may be made only with the approval of the commissioner".

The State Board of Education votes only on new charters the commissioner proposes. Each takes effect unless, within 90 days, "a majority of the members of the board present and voting vote against the grant", under §12.101(b-0).

More vetoes by December 31, 2027 are uncertain. Clark and Reveles voted against nearly every applicant on named roll calls in 2025 and 2026, the board minutes show. Pérez-Díaz voted to allow several after calling for a halt in 2018.

Each party holds seven seats with District 8 not called, the Texas Tribune reported as of November 5, 2026. District 8 decides which party has eight of the 15 seats, not how any member votes. Dana Van de Walker led there by 564 votes on the Secretary of State's count of November 4, 2026, and the canvass should settle the race. That result moves the charter-veto and curriculum estimates.

What to watch: the District 8 result when the state's official count, the canvass, ends by December 7, 2026, under a Secretary of State advisory, and the next commissioner's charter decisions.

Curriculum, library books and religion in schools. Hinojosa and Johnson voted against Senate Bill 10 of 2025, which requires the Ten Commandments to be displayed in classrooms, the House and Senate journals record. Johnson said as a candidate that he would not defend the law because he considers it unconstitutional. He would not defend it while appeals continue, as reported by KTRE.

Repeal of that law or of the library laws, House Bill 900 of 2023 and Senate Bill 13 of 2025, is very unlikely by May 31, 2027. Repeal needs the Senate.

We rate it likely that the attorney general's office stops arguing in court that the Ten Commandments law is constitutional, by December 31, 2027.

That would not repeal or suspend the law. Schools must still comply unless a court blocks it, and Senate Bill 10 still makes defending sued schools a duty of the office. Court rulings are outside these estimates.

The State Board's 2026 social studies standards and its reading list with Bible stories stay unless a board majority votes to reopen them. That is uncertain by December 31, 2027, and depends on who wins District 8.

What to watch: the attorney general's filings in those appeals once Johnson takes office, and the District 8 result.

Teacher preparation and certification. We found no statement on teacher residencies from any of the 20 people here. We found no pledge from Hinojosa that names a certification rule, program or funding source.

The State Board for Educator Certification writes the rules, and the governor appoints its 11 voting members with Senate consent, under chapter 21 of the Education Code. The State Board of Education can reject, but not change, a certification rule by two-thirds of members present and voting within 90 days, under §21.042.

We rate a substantial change in the rules unlikely by December 31, 2027, because we found no pledge on certification rules. That silence is not evidence that nothing will change: the estimate rests on who sits on the certification board in 2027.

House Bill 2's teacher-preparation allotment, described in a Texas Education Agency presentation, is very likely to be funded as designed for fiscal years 2028 and 2029, by June 20, 2027. Every winner who voted on the bill voted for it at least once, the House and Senate journals record. We found no group opposing the funding.

What to watch: the February 1, 2027 expiry of a third of the certification board's seats under §21.034, and Hinojosa's nominees. Members whose successors are not confirmed may stay until the 2029 regular session ends, under article XVI, section 17.

Higher education. Hinojosa plans to appoint university regents who would extend tuition grants to housing, food, transportation and textbooks, a Texas Tribune guide republished by High Plains Public Radio reports.

Repeal of Senate Bill 17 of 2023, on diversity offices, or Senate Bill 37 of 2025, on faculty governance, is very unlikely by May 31, 2027. Repeal needs the Senate, as the Texas Tribune describes. We make no estimate on regents, who need two-thirds of senators present under the constitution, because we found too few comparable cases.

What to watch: regents' seats expiring in February 2027, 11 according to KBTX and 20 according to the Tribune.

Not confirmed, and sources that could not be opened

We could not confirm these reported items on any page we could read. We list them so a reader can follow them up. None is used as fact in the profiles.

  • Talarico: an April 2026 Texas Observer essay on campaign money from Leadership for Educational Equity and on Teach For America's summer training institute.

  • Talarico: contributions from John and Laura Arnold.
  • Johnson: a report that he tried to remove vouchers from House Bill 100 in 2023.
  • Johnson: an October 2026 Atlantic interview on defending laws.
  • Johnson, Eckhardt, Ellis and Kelly: Houston Federation of Teachers endorsements listed only by third-party or aggregator sites.
  • Eckhardt: a report that she would "immediately curtail" the comptroller's spending reviews of Prosper ISD and other districts.
  • Flores: a report that he called vouchers "unconstitutional".
  • Van de Walker: a 2026 primary-guide answer calling for "routes to alternate certification that actually work" and an end to vouchers.
  • Pérez-Díaz and Reveles: 2024 Texas AFT endorsements known only from aggregator sites.
  • Reveles: a KVIA quotation on certification.

We could not open or read these sources:

  • Posts on X. Hinojosa's accounts returned an access error. We read Goodwin's and Talarico's posts only where news articles or campaign pages embedded them. Johnson's and Eckhardt's could not be retrieved.
  • Facebook, Instagram, Threads and TikTok accounts, which require a login, for most people in this document, including all four judges and most State Board members.
  • The New York Times profile of Talarico cited by the Daily Wire, two Texas Observer pages about Hinojosa and Talarico, a KERA page on Eckhardt and a Texas Monthly interview with Hinojosa.
  • Tucker's two Ballotpedia questionnaires and Van de Walker's 2026 primary guide.
  • A Texas Association of School Administrators table on a 2020 charter vote by Pérez-Díaz. It reportedly shows a different position from the one in the board minutes, and we did not read it.
  • Aggregator sites listing judicial and State Board endorsements.
